questionText: The lecture mentions that the iterative nature of 'code design' within the  Design-Prototype-Evaluate stage differs from 'interface design' iteration because:

options.text: Code design iterations are always longer.
Code design iterations do not require end-user feedback.
Interface design iterations are performed within the design team.
Code design iterations are not iterative at all.

explanation: The lecture states, 'Although that design of code is also iterative but that iteration does not  require end user feedback instead those iterations are performed within the design team.'

questionText: What is the primary concern in interactive software development, as repeatedly  emphasized in the lecture?
explanation: The lecture states, 'As we have repeatedly emphasized this brings us to the concept of user  centric or user centred design.'

questionText: If, during the Design-Prototype-Evaluate cycle, a prototype is built and user  feedback is taken, what is the next immediate step if changes are still required?

options.text: Refine the design and go for prototype building again.

explanation: The lecture describes the iterative nature: 'Based on the feedback we refine the design again  go for prototype building. And so on till we find out that no further changes in the design is required.'

questionText: Which of the following is a characteristic of the 'Empirical Study' stage?

options.text: It is an ad hoc process.
It requires a systematic and scientific approach for usability testing.
It is the first stage of the life cycle.

explanation: The lecture states, 'And that requires a systematic and scientific approach which is generally  called empirical research or empirical study... this is not an ad hoc process it requires systematic testing  approaches.'

questionText: The lecture suggests that a good design before implementation is crucial  because:

options.text: It makes the empirical study unnecessary.
It ensures the code is written faster.
Modifying the design later, which involves changing code, is technically costly in terms of  manpower.
It allows for more ad hoc testing.

explanation: The lecture states, 'before we go for implementation we try to get as good a design as possible.  So that we do not need to modify the design later then it will involve changing the code also which is  technically costly in terms of manpower.'

questionText: Consider a scenario where a software development team is using the interactive  system life cycle. They have completed the Design-Prototype-Evaluate cycle and  moved to implementation. After code testing, they conduct an empirical study and  find significant usability issues. What is the most appropriate and likely next step  according to the lecture?

options.text: Deploy the system immediately and address issues in maintenance.
Go back to the Design-Prototype-Evaluate cycle to refine the interface design.
Re-do the code testing to ensure no bugs exist.
Terminate the project due to high costs.

explanation: The lecture states, 'Based on the findings in this stage [empirical study] it may be possible that  we go back to this cycle [Design-Prototype-Evaluate cycle].'

questionText: What is the primary difference between the interactive system life cycle and the  classical waterfall model regarding user involvement?

options.text: The waterfall model involves users more actively.
The interactive system life cycle explicitly takes users into account at various stages.
The waterfall model only involves users during deployment.

explanation: The lecture states, 'taking into account the users is not explicitly the concern of the waterfall  model,' while the interactive life cycle is designed to 'take into account user feedback.'

questionText: The lecture mentions that the 'design of the interface and interaction' should be  quickly evaluated. This implies that:

options.text: The prototypes built for this evaluation should be simple and quick to achieve.
User feedback is not very important at this stage.
The design should be finalized without any changes.

explanation: The lecture states, 'our early evaluation and prototyping should be simpler to carry out. So  those should be quickly achievable. So that less time is required to build a prototype or to evaluate a  prototype.'

questionText: What is the main reason for the iterative nature of the Design-Prototype- Evaluate cycle?

options.text: To speed up the coding process.
To allow for continuous refinement of the interface design based on user feedback.
To reduce the number of stages in the life cycle.
To ensure the system is efficient.

explanation: The lecture explains, 'Based on the feedback we refine the design again go for prototype  building. And so on till we find out that no further changes in the design is required.'

questionText: If the interactive system life cycle is not followed properly in its earlier stages,  what could be a severe consequence mentioned?

options.text: The project might be completed ahead of schedule.
It may lead to non-delivery of the product.
The empirical study will be less costly.
The code will be more efficient.

explanation: The lecture warns, 'In fact it may lead to non-delivery of product also' if earlier stages are not  done properly, leading to multiple repetitions of costly loops.

questionText: Which of the following scenarios would most likely trigger an infrequent  iteration back to the Requirement Gathering stage in the interactive system life cycle?

options.text: A minor bug found during code testing.
Significant, fundamental issues with the product's core purpose identified during an empirical  study.
A design team brainstorming session for code optimization.
A quick prototype evaluation revealing a minor UI tweak.

explanation: The lecture mentions that going back to the requirement stage from the Design-Prototype- Evaluate cycle (which is influenced by empirical study findings) is 'not very frequent.' This implies that  such a drastic step would only be taken for fundamental issues, not minor bugs or UI tweaks.

questionText: The lecture states that the interactive system life cycle refines the classical  waterfall model to suit what purpose?

options.text: To suit the purpose of user-centric design.
To reduce the overall development time.
To make the process more linear.

explanation: The lecture states, 'we can refine this life cycle to suit our purpose... for implementation of  user centric design approach.'

questionText: What is the primary difference between 'prototype testing' and 'empirical study'  as described in the lecture?

options.text: Prototype testing is for code efficiency, empirical study is for usability.
Prototype testing is an early evaluation of interface design, while empirical study is a  systematic usability test of the implemented system with end-users.
Prototype testing involves end-users, empirical study involves only the design team.
Prototype testing is costly, empirical study is quick and simple.

explanation: The lecture describes early evaluation/prototype testing as part of the iterative design cycle  for the interface, while empirical study is a later, systematic, and costly usability test of the *implemented*  system. It also states, 'these testing approaches are totally different from what we have employed for  prototype testing or code testing.'

questionText: What is one of the core design concerns in interactive software development?
explanation: The lecture mentions, 'what are the code design concerns in the interactive software  development? And also we have got some idea of software engineering life cycles... our core concern here  is usability.'

questionText: The lecture advises that during the 'Implementation' stage, one should aim for a  good design beforehand. This is to prevent:

options.text: The need for any code testing.
Costly modifications to the code and design later due to manpower.
The empirical study from being too easy.
The requirement gathering stage from being too long.

explanation: The lecture states, 'before we go for implementation we try to get as good a design as possible.  So that we do not need to modify the design later then it will involve changing the code also which is  technically costly in terms of manpower.'

questionText: If a development team strictly followed the classical waterfall model for an  interactive system, and a critical usability flaw was discovered during system  integration and testing, what would be the most problematic consequence according  to the lecture's critique of the waterfall model?

options.text: The flaw would be easily fixed as part of the linear process.
The team would have to go back to an earlier stage (e.g., design or requirements), making the  process 'messy' and difficult to visualize.
The flaw would be ignored until the maintenance stage.
The project would automatically restart from the feasibility study.

explanation: The lecture explicitly states, 'after coding while going for testing. We find out some issue then  we may have to go back to this stage. We may also need to go back to this stage directly rather than going  in the design stage after again system testing, we may need to go back to unit level or design or  requirement stage. So; too much iteration which makes it difficult to visualize the overall process and  creates confusion.'

questionText: What is the primary difference in focus between the classical waterfall model  and the interactive system life cycle?

options.text: Waterfall focuses on efficiency, interactive focuses on usability.
Waterfall focuses on usability, interactive focuses on efficiency.
Waterfall focuses on deployment, interactive focuses on design.
Waterfall focuses on maintenance, interactive focuses on coding.

explanation: Refer to Week 1 lecture materials.

questionText: The lecture mentions that the 'design of the interface and interaction' involves  the point of view of the end-user. This is crucial because:

options.text: End-users are responsible for coding the interface.
The interface must be easy to use and understandable for its intended audience.
End-users provide the budget for the project.
End-users are primarily concerned with system efficiency.

explanation: The lecture states, 'One is design of the interface that is design of the interface and interaction  from the point of view of the end user... the software that we develop should be easy to use in other words  it should be usable for the intended users.'

questionText: What term is used synonymously with 'interactive systems' in the context of this  course?
explanation: The lecture states, 'interactive systems and human computer interfaces will be using  simultaneously and synonymously.'

questionText: The primary purpose of gathering usability requirements is to ensure that a  software product is:
explanation: The lecture emphasizes that the goal is to develop a system 'usable for lay persons or layman  users' and that 'usability is very important' for them.

questionText: Which of the following is the correct sequence of stages in the interactive  development life cycle as discussed in the lecture?

options.text: Feasibility study, Design/Prototype/Evaluate, Requirement gathering, Implementation
Requirement gathering, Feasibility study, Design/Prototype/Evaluate, Deployment
Feasibility study, Requirement gathering/analysis/specification, Design/Prototype/Evaluate,  Code design
Code design, Implementation, Usability study, Feasibility study

explanation: The lecture outlines the stages as: 'First stage is feasibility study... Once it is found to be  feasible we go for the second stage that is requirement gathering analysis and specification. Once that is  done we enter into this design prototype evaluate cycle... So once we stabilize on the interface and  interaction design... then we go for code design.'

questionText: When considering requirements for a calendar app, which of the following  would NOT be considered a usability requirement?

options.text: The app should be easy for users to schedule events.
The app should provide clear visual feedback for user actions.
The app should be developed using Java.
The app should allow users to easily set reminders.

explanation: The lecture explicitly states that 'what programming languages we should use that depends  on the kind of manpower available and their skill. So again that is of part of the feasibility study stage...  usability has nothing to do with platform or programming language.'

questionText: In user-centered design, the design is primarily based on:

options.text: The developer's preferred programming language and tools.
The user's abilities, context, goals, or needs.
The system's technical specifications and performance metrics.
The project's budget and timeline constraints.

explanation: The lecture defines user-centered design as 'where the design is supposed to be based on a  user's abilities, context, goals or needs.'

questionText: The Dilbert comic strip discussed in the lecture illustrates a tendency among  developers to:

options.text: Prioritize user needs over technical complexity.
Design systems that are simple and intuitive for end-users.
Develop products based on their own understanding and interests rather than actual user  study.
Always seek user feedback during the design process.

explanation: The lecture explains, 'this comic strip essentially indicates that developers may be having a  tendency to go for a design or development of a product in a way such that it is not correlated with the user  characteristics. Developer may like to develop as per his or her own or the teams own understanding of the  user rather than actually studying the user.'

questionText: Non-functional requirements (NFRs) are best described as:

options.text: System characteristics that can be expressed as functions with well-defined input and output.
Requirements related to the quality attributes of the system or software.
Requirements that are only considered during the deployment phase.
Requirements that are solely focused on the system's core functionalities.

explanation: The lecture states, 'Non-functional requirements... are system characteristics that cannot be  expressed as functions... Typically such requirements are related to the quality attributes of the system or  the software.'

questionText: Usability requirements are typically classified under which type of  requirements?
explanation: The lecture explicitly states, 'when we are talking of usability requirements these come under  non-functional requirement.'

questionText: Which category of non-functional requirements (NFRs) specifically includes  usability requirements?
explanation: The lecture lists 'interface issues' as one of the five broad categories of NFRs and then  clarifies, 'Among these our core concern is usability requirements which comes under this fifth category of  interface issues.'

questionText: Which of the following is NOT considered a performance-related non-functional  requirement?
explanation: The lecture lists 'reliability, security, response time' as performance-related NFRs.  Maintainability is mentioned under 'life cycle requirements' as a measure of design quality.

questionText: Physical constraints, availability of personnel, and system accessibility for  maintenance are examples of which category of non-functional requirements?
explanation: The lecture states, 'Then comes; the second category that is operating constraints so one of  these is physical constraints the size of the system. Then availability of personnel... skill level  considerations... also system accessibility for maintenance.'

questionText: Non-functional requirements related to immediate and/or long-term costs for  design, development, and implementation fall under which category?
explanation: The lecture states, 'Then comes the third category economic consideration here the non- functional requirements relate to immediate and or long term costs for design development and  implementation these three things.'

questionText: Maintainability, enhanceability, and portability are measures used to specify  requirements for the quality of the design, falling under which NFR category?
explanation: The lecture explains, 'Fourth category is life cycle requirements under this comes the design  quality requirement for the design quality... This quality of the design is measured in terms of  maintainability of the design, enhance ability of the design, portability of the design and so on.'

questionText: One significant advantage of properly specifying non-functional requirements is  that it:

options.text: Reduces the need for user feedback during development.
Ensures the software follows legal and adherence rules.
Allows developers to use any programming language they prefer.
Eliminates the need for a feasibility study.

explanation: The lecture lists as an advantage: 'that ensures that software follows legal and adherence  rules these are very important to maintain some standard.'

questionText: What is a potential severe consequence of NOT specifying non-functional  requirements properly or clearly before development begins?

options.text: The development team might become too efficient.
It may lead to time and cost overrun to fix issues later.
The system will automatically become more secure.
Users will be satisfied with any delivered product.

explanation: The lecture states, 'Also not doing so in time may lead to time and cost overrun to fix certain  issues later.'

questionText: In the interactive development life cycle, the feasibility study primarily  determines:

options.text: The specific programming language to be used.
Whether the development process is viable with available resources like manpower and cost.

explanation: The lecture describes the feasibility study as where 'we first try to see whether the  development process is feasible or not with respect to the available resources that includes manpower,  cost, time computing resources and so on.'

questionText: The 'design prototype evaluate cycle' in the interactive development life cycle  continues until:

options.text: The code design is fully implemented.
No further changes in design are required.
The final usability study is completed.

explanation: The lecture states, 'this cycle goes on until we reach a stage where no further changes in  design is required.'

questionText: After stabilizing on the interface and interaction design, the next step in the  interactive development life cycle is:
explanation: The lecture states, 'So once we stabilize on the interface and interaction design or rather once  we finalize the design then we go for code design.'

questionText: The final round of usability study for a product, often termed empirical study or  research, occurs after:
explanation: The lecture states, 'Once the testing is over and we get a working system we then have to go  for a final round of usability study for the product.'

questionText: Which of the following best characterizes a system-centered design approach?

options.text: Focus on what the user needs and expects.
Design based on the developer's expertise and interests.
Prioritizing ease of use for end-users.

explanation: The lecture describes system-centered design as where 'the main concerns of the developer  are what can I as a developer? Easily build on this platform... What do I as a programmer find interesting...  the concern is about the developers own expertise skill and interest rather than the user’s needs.'

questionText: In the calendar app example, the question 'How are we going to store the  information, should we use some RDBMS tools?' is primarily related to:
explanation: The lecture clarifies, 'This actually relates to the design of the system rather than requirement  for the system.'

questionText: The two main objectives in the requirement gathering, analysis, and  specification stage, concerning usability, are:

options.text: To implement the system and test it.
To identify requirements and convert them to system specifications.
To deploy the product and maintain it.
To conduct a feasibility study and code design.

explanation: The lecture states, 'first thing is we need to identify the requirements and second thing is we  need to convert it to some system specifications.'

questionText: A requirement that can be specified as a function with a well-defined input and  output is called a:
explanation: The lecture defines functional requirements: 'if a requirement can be specified as a function  where there is some well-defined input and well defined output then we call it as a functional  requirement.'

questionText: The 'interface issues' category of non-functional requirements deals with how a  system interfaces with:

options.text: Its environment, users, and other systems.

explanation: The lecture states, 'this nfr deals with how system is to interface with its environment users  and other systems.'

questionText: Specifying non-functional requirements properly contributes to achieving:

options.text: A complex system that challenges users.
Good user experience and ease of operating the software.
Faster development cycles by skipping user feedback.
A system that only satisfies developers.

explanation: The lecture states, 'Together all whatever we have mentioned ensures that at the end we get a  product which achieves good user experience and ease of operating the software by the user as well as the  technicians.'

questionText: The lecture emphasizes that not everything that comes to mind when thinking  about building a system is a requirement. Some queries may be related to:

options.text: Feasibility of the project or design of the system.

explanation: The lecture states, 'while going for identifying requirements we should be very careful  whether what we are identifying are related to the feasibility of the project or design of the system or  testing of the system so everything is not requirement.'

questionText: The 'design prototype evaluate cycle' is described as working in a cycle because:

options.text: It is only performed once at the beginning of the project.
It involves refining the design and prototype based on feedback until stabilization.
It is an optional stage that can be skipped.
It only focuses on the aesthetic aspects of the interface.

explanation: The lecture explains, 'Based on feedback we refine the design then again refine the prototype  or create a new prototype for the revised design. Which again is evaluated and this cycle goes on until we  reach a stage where no further changes in design is required.'

questionText: For interactive systems intended for non-expert users or laypersons, what is  considered very important?
explanation: The lecture states, 'here we are dealing with interactive systems that are to be used by non- expert users or laypersons and for them usability is very important.'

questionText: Not specifying non-functional requirements properly or clearly may lead to:
explanation: The lecture states, 'Not specifying the non-functional requirements properly or clearly may  also lead to inconsistent software which is not a desirable outcome.'

questionText: The 'interface issues' category of NFRs includes specifications for:

options.text: External system interfaces (hardware/software) and usability requirements.

explanation: The lecture states, 'it includes specification of this particular non-functional requirement  includes external system interface in terms of hardware and software requirements or in other words  peripheral devices or API’s. So how to interact with the external systems and usability requirements that is  what are the requirements to make the system usable.'

questionText: In a system-centered design approach, which of the following is typically NOT a  primary concern for the developer?

options.text: What can I easily build on this platform?
What do I as a programmer find interesting?
What is required by the user?
What can I create from available tools?

explanation: The lecture contrasts system-centered design with user-centered design, stating that in  system-centered design, the concerns are 'what can I as a developer? Easily build on this platform rather  than what is required by the user.'

questionText: Why does the lecture often use the term 'interactive system' for brevity?

options.text: To distinguish it from human-computer interfaces.
Because it is a more modern term.
To imply a system without human interaction.

explanation: The lecture states, 'most of the time we will be using the term interactive system for brevity  which will refer to human computer interfaces.'

questionText: In the 'design prototype evaluate cycle,' prototyping is done for:

options.text: Quick feedback on the quality and usability of the design.

explanation: The lecture states, 'that design is prototyped for quick feedback on the quality of the design  and usability of the design.'

questionText: According to the lecture, when should non-functional requirements be clearly  specified?

options.text: Only after the product has been deployed.
At the beginning stage, before development begins.
Only if issues arise during testing.

explanation: The lecture states, 'at the beginning stage all these non-functional requirements should be  clearly specified as much as possible.'

questionText: What is NOT a part of feasibility study?
explanation: The feasibility study focuses on resources like 'manpower, cost, time computing resources.'  User goals and needs are central to user-centered design and requirement gathering, not feasibility.

questionText: In the requirement gathering, analysis, and specification stage, the analysis  component is crucial for:

options.text: Converting gathered usability requirements into system specifications.

explanation: The lecture states, 'whatever usability requirements we gather or identify we need to analyze  them so that we can convert them to some specification system specification.'

questionText: In the context of defining non-functional requirements, a 'function' is described  as:

options.text: Any task performed by the user.
A process that takes some input and produces some output.
A quality attribute of the system.

explanation: The lecture explains, 'whenever there is a function it takes some input and produces some  output.'

questionText: The non-functional requirement of 'reliability' addresses:

options.text: How quickly the system responds to user input.
How to ensure the product is dependable and performs consistently.
The security measures implemented in the system.
The cost-effectiveness of the system's maintenance.

explanation: The lecture describes reliability as 'which says that how to ensure that the product is reliable  how we can ensure that.'

questionText: Specifying non-functional requirements helps ensure the system's performance  and:
explanation: The lecture states, 'It also ensures a product that is reliable, available on demand; ensure  performance as well as scalability of the system.'

questionText: If non-functional requirements are not specified, it may lead to unsatisfied  developers because:

options.text: They will have too much freedom in design.
They will not be given a clear idea of what to develop.
They will be forced to meet user expectations.
The project will be completed too quickly.

explanation: The lecture states, 'developers will not be given clear idea of what they need to develop then  at the end if they are told that whatever they have developed does not meet certain requirements then  definitely that will not be very satisfying for them.'

questionText: The primary focus of the current lecture series, 'Lec 5: Usability Requirements,'  primarily focuses on:
explanation: The lecture title is 'Usability Requirements' and the introduction states, 'So essentially it will  deal with how to gather requirements to ensure that our product is usable.'

questionText: In the Dilbert comic strip, the manager's response to Dilbert's complex system  idea was:

options.text: To reject it and demand a simple interface.
To support it and suggest even more complexity.

explanation: The lecture states, 'it appears that the manager is supportive of this idea and he also adds  along with this complexity in the system that, make the system so. So that the customer have to reboot or  the user have to reboot after every typographical error.'

questionText: What is NOT a quality attribute for design quality?
explanation: The lecture lists 'maintainability of the design, enhance ability of the design, portability of the  design' as measures of design quality. Security is a performance-related NFR.

questionText: For the purpose of this course, the lecture states that the feasibility study stage  will be skipped, assuming that:

options.text: It is not important for interactive systems.
The development is already found to be feasible.
It will be covered in a later, more advanced course.
It is the responsibility of the client, not the developer.

explanation: The lecture states, 'we will skip the first stage that is feasibility study... We will assume that  whatever we discuss is on the basis of the assumption that the further development is feasible already that  is found out to be feasible.'

questionText: Besides good user experience for the end-user, specifying NFRs also ensures  ease of operating the software for:

options.text: The technicians who maintain the software.

explanation: The lecture states, 'achieves good user experience and ease of operating the software by the  user as well as the technicians who are tasked to maintain the software.'

questionText: In the context of this lecture, what does the term 'product' primarily refer to?
explanation: The lecture clarifies, 'here by product we mean a software application.'

questionText: What happens if the final usability study reveals issues with the interface and  interaction design?

options.text: Going back to the design/prototype/evaluate cycle to refine the design.

explanation: The lecture states, 'it is possible that we may find some more issues with our design of the  interface and interaction. So it may require us although infrequently but still sometimes we may need to go  back to this cycle to refine our design and then again recode retest and then finalize the product.'

questionText: When the lecture uses the term 'interface' in the context of NFRs, it is referring  to:

options.text: Only the visual layout of the system.
Two conceptual things: interface and interaction.

explanation: The lecture clarifies, 'whenever we are using the term interface we are referring to 2  conceptual things one is interface one is interaction so this is related to interfaces as well as interaction.'

questionText: Not specifying non-functional requirements in time or before development  begins may even lead to:

options.text: Total wastage of time and cost by not delivering the product at all.
A product that is too simple.

explanation: The lecture states, 'it may even lead to not delivering the product at all total wastage of time  and cost.'

questionText: After discussing non-functional requirements, the lecture indicates that  subsequent lectures will also cover:
explanation: The lecture concludes by stating, 'Now that specification is generally called as functional  requirements. So we shall also learn about functional requirements in subsequent lectures.'

questionText: What is the primary objective of Contextual Inquiry?

options.text: To lecture users on how to perform tasks efficiently.
To observe users performing tasks in their natural work setting.
To conduct structured interviews with users about their preferences.
To gather feedback on a prototype in a controlled lab environment.

explanation: The primary objective of contextual inquiry is to watch and observe users while they are  performing tasks in their natural work setting or work context.

questionText: In Contextual Inquiry, what is the role of interviews?

options.text: They are the sole method for data collection.
They are used as a primary method, replacing observations.
They act as a supporting mechanism for observations to clarify behaviors.
They are conducted only after the product is deployed.

explanation: In contextual inquiry, observations are the primary method, and interviews are used as a  supporting mechanism of observations to clarify certain behavioral issues or activities.

questionText: When was the importance of Contextual Inquiry in user-centered design first  highlighted?
explanation: The importance of contextual inquiry in user-centered design was highlighted way back in  1988.

questionText: Why is it potentially misleading to refer to Contextual Inquiry solely as a semi- structured interview?

options.text: Because it only involves structured interviews.
Because it primarily involves observations, with interviews as support.
Because it is a fully automated data collection method.
Because it is only used for feasibility studies.

explanation: It may be somewhat misleading because contextual inquiry is not only an interview; instead,  it involves both interview and observations, with observations being the primary method.

questionText: According to the ISO definition, usability is the extent to which a product can be  used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and  satisfaction in what?
explanation: The ISO definition of usability states it is 'the extent to which a product can be used by  specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a specified  context of use.'

questionText: What is the typical duration for a contextual inquiry process?
explanation: Generally, the contextual inquiry process continues for 1 to 2 hours, as longer durations may  not be desirable for users and may not yield much new behavioral knowledge.

questionText: What knowledge can designers gain from observations made during contextual  inquiry?

options.text: Only technical specifications of existing systems.
Task domain, work culture, and physical and social constraints at the workplace.

explanation: Observations enable designers to learn about the task domain, work culture, and physical and  social constraints that are prevalent at the workplace, as well as various idiosyncratic attributes of user  behavior.

questionText: In the master-apprentice model of contextual inquiry, who is considered the  'master'?
explanation: In the master-apprentice model, it is assumed that the users are masters, and the observers  need to learn from the users, acting as apprentices.

questionText: What should observers strictly avoid doing during contextual inquiry, according  to the master-apprentice model?

options.text: Lecturing users on how to do things.

explanation: Observers should act as apprentices and treat users as masters, learning from them. They  should strictly avoid the tendency to teach or lecture users about how to do things.

questionText: Which of the following is NOT one of the five broad stages of Contextual Inquiry?
explanation: The five stages of contextual inquiry are Plan, Initiate, Execute, Close, and Reflect. Implement  is not listed as one of these stages.

questionText: What is a key activity performed during the 'Plan' stage of Contextual Inquiry?

options.text: Sending thank you notes to participants.
Identifying goals of observation and arranging for recording.
Observing users in their natural work setting.

explanation: The plan stage involves identification of the goals of observation, knowledge gathering about  the task domain, arrangements for recording observations, and identification of users and the  observational setup.

questionText: Why is the 'Initiate' stage considered crucial in Contextual Inquiry?

options.text: It is when the actual data collection occurs.
It ensures users willingly participate by establishing communication and obtaining permission.
It involves analyzing the collected data.
It is where design recommendations are formulated.

explanation: The initiate stage is crucial because it involves contacting authorities for permission and  establishing open communication with end-users so that they willingly participate in the observation  process.

questionText: What happens during the 'Execute' stage of Contextual Inquiry?
explanation: The third stage, 'Execute,' is the actual data collection stage where observation takes place  and data is collected.

questionText: What is the primary reason for properly conducting the 'Close' stage of  Contextual Inquiry?

options.text: To immediately start the design phase.
To ensure future engagement of participants for further studies.

explanation: The close stage is important because if not properly done, participants may not agree to  engage in future data collection or empirical studies if needed. It involves sending thank you notes.

questionText: What is the main activity in the 'Reflect' stage of Contextual Inquiry?

options.text: Analyzing collected data to identify design goals.

explanation: In the reflect stage, the data collected through observations are analyzed to identify the  design goals.

questionText: What is the purpose of the Affinity Diagram method in the context of Contextual  Inquiry?

options.text: To analyze collected observational data and identify design goals.
To record user activities in passive mode.

explanation: The Affinity Diagram method is a technique available to analyze the data collected during  contextual inquiry and find out design goals.

questionText: Which of the following is the correct sequence of steps in the Affinity Diagram  method?

options.text: Display ideas, Generate ideas, Sort ideas, Create group header, Draw diagram.
Generate ideas, Display ideas, Sort ideas into groups, Create group header, Draw finished  Affinity Diagram.
Sort ideas, Generate ideas, Display ideas, Create group header, Draw diagram.
Create group header, Generate ideas, Display ideas, Sort ideas, Draw diagram.

explanation: The method contains five steps: Generate idea, Display ideas, Sort ideas into groups, Create  group header, and finally Draw the finished Affinity Diagram.

questionText: In the 'Generate ideas' step of the Affinity Diagram method, what typically  constitutes an 'idea'?

options.text: A raw observation or note recorded during inquiry.

explanation: Ideas are generated after or during observations, representing the raw observations or notes  recorded during the inquiry process.

questionText: How are ideas typically 'displayed' in the Affinity Diagram method for analysis?

options.text: On a whiteboard or wall using sticky notes.

explanation: Ideas are displayed by pasting them on some surface, such as a wall or whiteboard, often  using sticky notes, for team members to review.

questionText: What is the criterion for 'sorting ideas into groups' in the Affinity Diagram  method?

options.text: Grouping ideas by the time they were observed.
Grouping ideas by the observer who recorded them.
Grouping behavioral observations that are similar in nature.
Grouping ideas based on their perceived difficulty of implementation.

explanation: The third stage is to sort the observations into groups, meaning behavioral observations that  are similar in nature should be sorted into groups.

questionText: What is the purpose of 'creating group headers' in the Affinity Diagram method?

options.text: To assign a unique ID to each observation.
To summarize the common theme or issue represented by a group of observations.
To categorize observations by user demographics.
To mark observations that are irrelevant.

explanation: Group headers are assigned names that actually give some idea of the issues, the design  issues, or the usability issues that need to be addressed to make the product usable.

questionText: What is the primary outcome of the Affinity Diagram method when applied to  contextual inquiry data?

options.text: A set of design recommendations or rationales.
A list of user names and contact information.

explanation: The outcome of the Affinity Diagram method is a set of design rationales or it may lead to a  set of functional requirements.

questionText: Contextual Inquiry is primarily an observation-based approach. What is the role  of semi-structured interviews within this approach?

options.text: To provide clarifications on observed user behaviors or activities.

explanation: Contextual inquiry is primarily an observation to observe user behavior in their work setting,  and semi-structured interviews can be used as a supporting tool to get clarifications on certain user  behaviors or activities.

questionText: In the 'active mode' of contextual inquiry, what is the observer's physical  presence like?

options.text: The observer is not physically present.
The observer is physically present in the work setting.
The observer is present remotely via video conference.
The observer is present only during interviews, not observations.

explanation: In the active mode, the observer is physically present in the work setting where the users are  being observed.

questionText: How are user activities recorded in the 'passive mode' of contextual inquiry?

options.text: The observer takes handwritten notes while physically present.
User activities are recorded or videotaped and reviewed later by the observer.
Users self-report their activities in a diary.
The observer directly interacts with users to understand their activities.

explanation: In passive mode, the observer is not physically present; instead, the user activities are  recorded or videotaped, and the observer reviews those videos or recordings at a later time.

questionText: Why is 'knowledge about the user' considered a very important aspect in the  conceptualization to implementation of an interactive system?

options.text: To ensure the system is technically complex.
To understand the end-users' needs and build a usable product.
To reduce the cost of the project.

explanation: Knowledge about the user (end-users or laymen users) is very important because it helps in  understanding their needs and building a usable product that addresses their goals in a specified context of  use.

questionText: In the calendar app example, what two important activities were observed that  helped in designing a usable product for managerial staff?

options.text: Sending emails and browsing the internet.
Setting meeting dates and setting reminders.

explanation: In the calendar app example, it was observed that intended users frequently perform two  important activities: set meeting dates and set reminders. This knowledge helps in deciding what features  to keep in the app.

questionText: What is the main type of requirement that Contextual Inquiry helps to gather?
explanation: Contextual inquiry is a specific approach to gather usability requirements from end-users.

questionText: In which stage of the interactive system development life cycle is Contextual  Inquiry primarily used?
explanation: Contextual inquiry is used in the requirement gathering stage of the interactive system  development life cycle, with an emphasis on gathering usability requirements.

questionText: The lecture mentions that without specific knowledge about target user behavior,  designers might come up with many alternatives based on intuition. How does  Contextual Inquiry help overcome this?

options.text: By providing a standardized list of features.
By offering specific knowledge derived from observing user behavior in their work settings.
By limiting the number of design alternatives.

explanation: Contextual inquiry provides specific knowledge about user behavior in their work settings,  which helps designers understand what features are needed, rather than relying on intuition.

questionText: Why is identifying specific design goals from collected contextual inquiry data  often not trivial?

options.text: Because the data is always incomplete.
Because there may be lots of data, making analysis complex.

explanation: Identifying specific design goals from collected data is not easy because there may be lots of  data, and going through it to identify specific design goals is generally not very trivial.

questionText: In the note-taking application example, which observation was grouped under  the header 'Navigation in notebook or notebook application'?

options.text: Multi-level organization of notes not possible.
Erasing contents is a daunting task.

explanation: 'Multi-level organization of notes not possible' was grouped with 'sorting of lectures by dates  is torturous' and 'organization of course-wise notes difficult' under the header 'Navigation in notebook or  notebook application.'

questionText: For the note-taking application, which observations were combined under the  header 'Navigation in notes'?

options.text: Content relocation not possible and cannot insert images.
Difficult to search keywords in notes and navigation between different topics is cumbersome.
Text formatting should be handy and freehand drawing is not accurate.
Sorting of lectures by dates is torturous and multi-level organization of notes not possible.

explanation: The observations 'difficult to search keywords in notes' and 'navigation between different  topics is cumbersome' were combined into a group with the header 'Navigation in notes.'

questionText: Which observations were grouped under the header 'Note organization' in the  note-taking application example?

options.text: Cannot insert any images and text formatting should be handy.
Freehand drawing is not accurate and incorporating mathematical symbols not supported.
Erasing contents is a daunting task and content relocation not possible.
Multi-level organization of notes not possible and sorting of lectures by dates is torturous.

explanation: 'Erasing contents is a daunting task' and 'content relocation not possible in physical or pen  and paper based note taking approach' were considered to belong to the same group with the header 'Note  organization.'

questionText: The lecture states that the outcome of the Affinity Diagram method focuses on  'what we need.' What does it explicitly NOT focus on?

options.text: How to implement the particular thing that we need.

explanation: The lecture clarifies that the focus is on 'what we need to make the design usable rather than  how to implement the particular thing that we need.'

questionText: Which stage of the interactive system development life cycle is explicitly  mentioned as NOT being covered in detail in the lecture?
explanation: The lecture states, 'first stage is feasibility study which we are not covering in details here.'

questionText: After the requirement gathering stage, what is the next cycle mentioned in the  interactive system development life cycle?
explanation: After the requirement gathering stage, the cycle mentioned is 'design prototype evaluate  cycle,' involving the design stage, prototyping stage, and evaluation stage.

questionText: What does the design stage in the interactive system development life cycle  involve?

options.text: Both interface design and code design.

explanation: The design stage involves both interface design as well as code design.

questionText: What is the final stage mentioned in the interactive system development life  cycle, after coding, implementation, and testing?

options.text: Ascertaining usability through empirical study, then deployment and maintenance.

explanation: A final stage is to again ascertain the usability of the overall system through empirical study  and then, finally deployment and maintenance.

questionText: What was Contextual Inquiry referred to as in 1988?
explanation: At that time (1988), this technique used to be referred to as phenomenological research  method.

questionText: How can an observer capture observations in the active mode of contextual  inquiry?

options.text: Through handwritten notes, videography, or other comfortable methods.
By relying solely on user self-reports.

explanation: In active mode, the observer captures the observation in some form, either handwritten notes  or videography or something whichever the observer feels comfortable with.

questionText: Besides user preference, what is another reason mentioned for limiting  contextual inquiry to 1-2 hours?

options.text: Longer observations may reveal similar things without much gain in behavioral knowledge.
It is difficult to record data for longer periods.
The work setting changes too rapidly.

explanation: For a longer duration, observations may reveal similar things without much gain in  behavioral knowledge.

questionText: What specific aspect of the workplace, related to user behavior, can be learned  through contextual inquiry observations?

options.text: Various idiosyncratic attributes of the workplace with respect to user behavior and  participation.
The technical specifications of the software used.

explanation: Various idiosyncratic attributes of the workplace with respect to the user behavior and  participation can be learned through these observations.

questionText: Why is knowledge about the specific work context important for a designer?

options.text: To ensure the product is aesthetically pleasing.
To design a usable product, as work context is part of the usability definition.
To reduce the number of features in the product.

explanation: This knowledge is very important because the designer should be aware of the specific work  context, which is part of the definition of usability, to design a usable product.

questionText: In the note-taking application example, what types of tools were used to study  user behavior during contextual inquiry?

options.text: A physical pen and paper, a web application, and desktop software.

explanation: Three tools were used: a physical pen and paper-based note-taking, one web application  (notion.so), and xournal++ desktop software.

questionText: After displaying ideas, what is the next step that involves team members in the  Affinity Diagram method?

options.text: Brainstorming to sort similar observations into groups.

explanation: After displaying ideas, the team brainstorms to sort similar observations into groups.

questionText: The lecture mentions that Affinity Diagram output can lead to functional  requirements. How do these functional requirements relate to usability  requirements?

options.text: They are completely separate and unrelated.
They take care of usability requirements implicitly.
They are only concerned with system performance.

explanation: Affinity diagram output can be used to come up with functional requirements which will take  care of usability requirements implicitly.

questionText: Besides effectiveness and efficiency, what is the third component of usability  mentioned in the ISO definition?
explanation: The ISO definition of usability includes effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction.

questionText: What is the purpose of rehearsing the observation script multiple times during  the 'Plan' stage?

options.text: To ensure the observation is smoothly done.

explanation: All these (planning activities) can be converted to a script and can be rehearsed many times  before the actual observation takes place so that it is smoothly done.

questionText: What kind of communication should be established with end-users during the  'Initiate' stage of Contextual Inquiry?

options.text: Open communication to ensure willing participation.
Only one-way communication from observers to users.

explanation: In the initiate stage, open communication with the end-users should be established so that  they willingly participate in the observation process.

questionText: Which of the following is NOT considered a primary stage in the software  development lifecycle for interactive software, as discussed in the lecture?
explanation: The lecture states that the feasibility study stage is 'not very relevant for our core concepts'  and was not discussed in detail, unlike the other stages which are central to the interactive software  development lifecycle.

questionText: What is the primary characteristic of interactive software that necessitates a  specific software development lifecycle, according to the lecture?

options.text: It must be developed using object-oriented programming.
It is intended for expert users who understand technology.
It requires significant user feedback at different development stages.
It must always be deployed on cloud platforms.

explanation: The lecture emphasizes that interactive software is 'supposed to be used by layman users who  are not experts in the technology' and for them, 'we need to take into account various things most  importantly user feedbacks at different stages of development'.

questionText: Usability is categorized as which type of requirement?
explanation: The lecture explicitly states, 'whatever we have termed as usability requirement earlier is  also known as non-functional requirements.'

questionText: Why are non-functional requirements (NFRs) often difficult to formally specify?

options.text: They are too specific and detailed.
They are not relevant to system design.
They are not easily convertible to design requirements or implementation.
They only apply to non-interactive systems.

explanation: The lecture mentions, 'But one issue with non-functional requirements only is that these are  difficult to formally specify and unless they are properly specified... it is difficult to convert them to design  requirements or into a proper implementation of the system.'

questionText: Which of the following is NOT listed as a type of non-functional requirement in  the lecture?
explanation: The lecture lists performance related, operating constraints, economic considerations, life  cycle requirements, and interface issues as non-functional requirements. User interface design algorithms  are a method of implementation, not a requirement type.

questionText: What is the primary goal when formally specifying requirements, particularly  functional requirements?

options.text: To make them difficult for the development team to understand.
To ensure they are easy to understand and implement in the form of a program.
To focus solely on the user interface design.
To delay the implementation stage as much as possible.

explanation: The lecture states, 'our objective should be to have requirements which are easy to  understand and implement in the form of a program.'

questionText: Functional requirements specify a system in terms of what?

options.text: Its functions, defined by input, output, and purpose.
Its hardware specifications and network topology.
Its aesthetic appeal and color scheme.

explanation: The lecture defines functional requirements: 'functional requirements specify a system or the  requirements of the system in terms of functions. What are functions? Mathematically functions are  defined in terms of its input output and here also we specify the requirements in terms of functions that  take some specific input produces some specific output and these functions also typically has some purpose  mentioned in the specification.'

questionText: What does 'abstraction' mean in the context of functional requirement  specification?

options.text: Identifying how a function will be implemented.
Focusing on the visual design of the system.
Identifying black box functions by only specifying input and output, not implementation  details.
Creating a detailed algorithm for each function.

explanation: The lecture explains abstraction: 'We only need to identify black box functions to be  supported by the end product or the system. And in this black box functions we need to only specify the  input and output. So, in other words abstraction tells us that identify only the need rather than how to  achieve it.'

questionText: Why is decomposition and hierarchy important when identifying functions for  functional requirements?

options.text: It makes the specification more complex and difficult to manage.
It allows for a single, monolithic function to represent the entire system.
It helps better manage the description of the system by breaking it into functions and sub- functions.
It is only relevant for very simple systems.

explanation: The lecture states, 'we should decompose the entire requirement into some sort of hierarchy  of functions and sub functions. Otherwise it will be difficult and too complex to specify the functions... this  decomposition into hierarchical levels and the levels of the hierarchy help us better manage the  description or the functional description of the system.'

questionText: What is meant by 'exploratory style of definition' that should be avoided in  functional requirement specification?

options.text: Thinking abstractly about functions before implementation.
Implementing functions first and then trying to derive the functional hierarchy from them.
Focusing on the input and output of black box functions.
Creating a detailed design document before any coding.

explanation: Refer to Week 2 lecture materials.

questionText: What does the acronym SRS stand for in the context of software development?
explanation: The lecture explicitly states, 'what we get is called the SRS or software requirement  specification document. So SRS this acronym comes from these terms these words software requirement  specification.'

questionText: In an SRS document, what is the typical structure used to represent  requirements?

options.text: A flat list of all requirements without any grouping.
A hierarchical structure with level names like R1, R1.1.
A flowchart showing the execution order of functions.
A database schema of the system.

explanation: The lecture describes the SRS format: 'generally what is followed is a hierarchical structure  with some name given to the hierarchy levels like r 1, r 1.1 and so on.'

questionText: Which of the following components are typically included in a textual description  of a functional requirement in an SRS document?

options.text: Developer's name, project budget, and estimated completion date.
Level number, function name, input specification, output specification, and description.
Hardware requirements, operating system, and programming language.
User interface mockups and database design.

explanation: The lecture details the textual description format: 'textual description follows its own format  with level numbers r 1, r 1.1 etcetera and function name input specification output specification and some  function description.'

questionText: When specifying input and output for a functional requirement, what level of  detail is recommended at the FRS stage?

options.text: Very specific, including data types and exact formats.
As vague and open as possible, avoiding algorithmic details.
Only the data types, without mentioning the purpose.
Only the purpose, without mentioning any data.

explanation: The lecture advises, 'It should not be very specific because here still we are talking of black  boxes as functions so we are not going into the details of any algorithmic design. So our input should be  kept as much open as possible... Similarly for output we are not specifying the exact nature of the output  instead a broad idea of what the output should look like.'

questionText: What type of words should be avoided when specifying the input or output of a  function in an SRS document?

options.text: Action words that imply a process.

explanation: The lecture warns, 'One common mistake occasionally we perform is that when we are  specifying the output we also specify some functional words. For example here send one time password  output we may be tempted to write send one time password. Now the with the addition of the word send it  no longer remains an output rather it becomes a process in itself so try to avoid using this type of action  words in either input or output.'

questionText: In the example of the class note-taking application, 'Authentication' is presented  as what level of functional requirement?
explanation: The lecture shows 'Authentication' at the highest level of the hierarchy, alongside 'Notebook  Management' and 'Search in Notebook', indicating it's a top-level functional requirement.

questionText: Which of the following is a sub-function listed under 'Authentication' in the note- taking application example?
explanation: The lecture states, 'under authentication we have these 3 sub functions create new account  login and update password.'

questionText: The 'Update Password' function, under 'Authentication', can be further  decomposed into which sub-functions?

options.text: Send one time password and Set new password
Search by text and Search by date

explanation: The lecture provides the example: 'update password can have sub functions under it as well  for example there can be one sub function send one time password can be another sub function set new  password.'

questionText: What is the benefit of decomposing a high-level functional requirement like  'Notebook Management' into sub-functions?

options.text: It makes the overall requirements more complex and harder to understand.
It allows for a single, vague description for the entire function.
It makes it easier to specify input, output, and description for smaller, more manageable parts.
It eliminates the need for any textual specification.

explanation: The lecture explains, 'by decomposing we are able to better manage this complexity by  dividing it into sub function. So then now what we need to do is basically specify only the input output for  the sub functions which is much more easier compared to specifying everything for only one function.'

questionText: Under the 'Edit Note' function in the notebook management hierarchy, which of  these is a listed sub-function?
explanation: The lecture lists 'Under edit note we can have further decomposition add text, draw content,  insert image, manage table, delete content etcetera.'

questionText: What is the recommended practice for specifying input, output, and description  in an SRS document regarding hierarchical levels?

options.text: Only specify them for the highest-level functions.
Only specify them for the leaf-level functions.
Specify them for each and every function at every level of the hierarchy.
Specify them only if the function is complex.

explanation: The lecture states, 'It is generally preferable that higher level also you specify the input,  output and description optionally for each level function you should do that not only for the leaf level  notes... So at each level for every function you should ideally specify the input output and description for  each and every function in that level.'

questionText: When creating functional requirements, what is a good starting point, according  to the lecture?

options.text: Immediately writing code for the system.
Domain knowledge and discussion with clients.

explanation: The lecture mentions, 'functional requirements need not be created based on end user  studies. Some domain knowledge plus some discussion with the clients may be good starting point to create  the functional requirements.'

questionText: The lecture suggests that usability requirements, which are non-functional, can  be incorporated into the functional requirement hierarchy by:

options.text: Converting some of them into functions.
Listing them separately in a non-functional requirements document only.
Using them to define the system's hardware.

explanation: The lecture states, 'once usability requirements are available some of those requirements can  be converted to functions and put in the functional requirement hierarchy and subsequently included in  the SRS document.'

questionText: What is the purpose of keeping input and output specifications 'open-ended and  flexible' in the FRS stage?

options.text: To make the document intentionally vague and unhelpful.
To allow for interpretation and detailed decisions in later design and implementation stages.
To avoid any need for further design work.
To ensure the system can never be implemented.

explanation: The lecture explains, 'we should keep it open for interpretation at later stages of the  development life cycle. Because here we are not bothered about how the functions are to be implemented  rather what the function should do?'

questionText: Which of the following is a key characteristic of functional requirements?

options.text: They are difficult to understand and implement.
They specify the system in terms of its functions.
They are primarily concerned with system performance metrics.
They are always derived directly from user interface mockups.

explanation: The lecture states, 'functional requirements specify a system or the requirements of the  system in terms of functions.'

questionText: What is the role of the 'description' section for a functional requirement in an  SRS document?

options.text: To detail the exact algorithm for implementation.
To state the purpose of what the function does.
To list all possible error messages.
To specify the programming language to be used.

explanation: The lecture mentions, 'And then there is this optional section on description of the function.  So it says what the function does purpose simply says create a new account using user details and display  account creation message that is simply the purpose.'

questionText: The 'empirical study stage' in the interactive software development lifecycle is  primarily concerned with testing for:
explanation: The lecture states, 'Once the system is implemented we need to test it... we still need to test it  for usability. Which is one of the key concerns in our interactive systems and that is done in the empirical  study stage.'

questionText: Contextual inquiry is a method primarily used for:
explanation: The lecture mentions, 'We have gone through in the previous lecture one method of  requirement gathering particularly usability requirement gathering that is contextual inquiry.'

questionText: After gathering requirements using contextual inquiry, what tool is mentioned  for analyzing observations to identify design goals?
explanation: The lecture states, 'whatever we have gathered during contextual inquiry can be analyzed to  identify design goals or some such things through the reflect stage using various tools such as affinity  diagram method.'

questionText: Which of the following is an example of an 'interface issue' non-functional  requirement?

options.text: The system must process 100 transactions per second.
The system must be developed using Java.
The system must be usable by novice users.
The system must cost less than $10,000 to develop.

explanation: The lecture categorizes 'interface issues' as non-functional requirements and clarifies that  'software interface issues are generally termed as usability which belongs to this kind of non-functional  requirements.' Usability for novice users falls under this category.

questionText: What is the main difference between functional and non-functional requirements  in terms of specification?

options.text: Functional requirements are difficult to specify, while non-functional are easy.
Functional requirements are easy to understand and implement, while non-functional are  difficult to formally specify.
Non-functional requirements define system behavior, while functional requirements define  system quality.
There is no significant difference in their specification approach.

explanation: The lecture contrasts them by stating NFRs 'are difficult to formally specify' and 'are not very  much suitable to be converted to that proper way' for implementation, whereas FRs 'are easy to  understand and convert to codes'.

questionText: When defining functions, the lecture advises against starting to think about the  algorithm to implement them. Instead, what should be the focus?

options.text: Functions as black boxes with only input, output, and purpose.
The marketing strategy for the product.
The legal implications of the software.

explanation: The lecture states, 'We should not start thinking about the algorithm to implement the  functions rather we should think of functions as black boxes and only input and output need to be thought  of plus the purpose of the function.'

questionText: What is the significance of a 'functional hierarchy' in functional requirement  specification?

options.text: It restricts the number of functions a system can have.
It makes the system design more rigid and less adaptable.
It helps manage the complexity of specifying functions by organizing them into levels and sub- functions.
It is an optional step that provides no real benefit.

explanation: The lecture explains, 'it will be easier to manage the specification if we can think of the  functions in the form of a hierarchy of functions and sub functions rather than only one level that will  make things easier to manage.'

questionText: In the SRS notation R1.3.1, what does '1.3.1' represent?

options.text: The version number of the software.
A unique identifier for a non-functional requirement.
The hierarchical level and position of a sub-function.
The estimated time to implement the function.

explanation: The lecture describes this notation: 'hierarchical structure with some name given to the  hierarchy levels like r 1, r 1.1 and so on. And at each level or r where r 1.1 etcetera which indicates the  hierarchy each level represents a function.' R1.3.1 would be a sub-function of R1.3.

questionText: For the 'Create New Account' function, the input specification is simply 'user  information'. Why is this vague description acceptable at the FRS stage?

options.text: It indicates a lack of understanding of the requirement.
It allows flexibility for detailed design decisions later, as FRS focuses on 'what' not 'how'.
It is a placeholder for information that will never be defined.
It is a common error in functional specification.

explanation: The lecture states, 'it is possible to keep it vague at this stage because we are not going to  discuss about how to implement? So the flexibility should remain... So our input should be kept as much  open as possible.'

questionText: What is the consequence of using an action word like 'send' in an output  specification (e.g., 'send one time password')?

options.text: It makes the output specification more precise.
It correctly describes the data being output.
It incorrectly turns the output into a process or function itself.
It is a recommended practice for clarity.

explanation: The lecture warns, 'Now the with the addition of the word send it no longer remains an  output rather it becomes a process in itself so try to avoid using this type of action words in either input or  output if you are using action words then the description is wrong.'

questionText: The lecture mentions that the example functional hierarchy for the note-taking  app is 'not complete'. What does this imply about real-world functional requirement  specifications?

options.text: They are always incomplete and never finalized.
They should aim for comprehensive decomposition and specification of all functions.
They only need to cover the top-level functions.
They are primarily visual and do not require textual details.

explanation: The lecture implies completeness is a goal by stating, 'the more decomposition is the better for  specification. It will bring in clarity of thought if you have very less number of levels and everything in the  single level then it is generally considered to be not a good specification assuming. That the system is  complex.'

questionText: What is the primary concern of the 'coding and implementation stage' in the  SDLC?

options.text: Implementing finalized modules using programming languages.

explanation: The lecture states, 'Now those modules once finalized are to be implemented using  programming some sort of programming language that is the coding and implementation stage.'

questionText: Which stage of the SDLC is described as 'quite costly' and expected to be done  'once or twice at the most'?
explanation: The lecture refers to the empirical study stage: 'this stage is quite costly. However there is a  possibility that output of this stage can lead here and there can be a cycle. So once this study stage is  complete and we are assumed of the usability as well as executability of the system we go for deployment  and maintenance that is our last stage.'

questionText: What is the relationship between 'usability requirements' and 'non-functional  requirements'?

options.text: Usability requirements are a type of non-functional requirement.
Non-functional requirements are a type of usability requirement.
They are interchangeable terms for the same thing.

explanation: The lecture clarifies, 'whatever we have termed as usability requirement earlier is also  known as non-functional requirements. This is a term that is used to refer to requirements such as  usability and some other things so usability requirements are one type of non-functional requirements.'

questionText: The lecture emphasizes that functional requirements should be easy to  understand and 'convert to codes'. What does this imply about their nature?

options.text: They must be written in a specific programming language.
They should be precise enough to guide direct implementation.
They are only for documentation purposes, not implementation.
They are primarily concerned with user experience.

explanation: The lecture states, 'our objective should be to have requirements which are easy to  understand and implement in the form of a program... They have these properties that they are easy to  understand and convert to codes'. This implies a direct link to implementation.

questionText: What is the primary purpose of the 'design, prototype, evaluate cycle' in the SDLC  for interactive software?

options.text: To finalize the system's deployment strategy.
To implement the core business logic.
To iteratively refine the interfaces and interactions based on evaluation.
To conduct a feasibility study for the project.

explanation: The lecture describes this cycle: 'design, prototyping stage and evaluation of prototyping these  3 sub stages in a cycle constitute the design prototype evaluate cycle. Now here design refers to both design  of the interfaces as well as interactions and also design of the system in terms of modules.' The cyclical  nature implies iterative refinement.

questionText: When creating a functional hierarchy, what is generally considered a sign of a  poor specification for a complex system?

options.text: Having very few levels and everything in a single level.
Using clear and consistent naming conventions.
Specifying input and output for each function.

explanation: The lecture states, 'It will bring in clarity of thought if you have very less number of levels and  everything in the single level then it is generally considered to be not a good specification assuming. That  the system is complex.'

questionText: What is the main difference between a visual depiction of a functional hierarchy  and a textual SRS document?

options.text: The visual depiction is the formal specification, while the textual document is informal.
The visual depiction is for internal use only, while the textual document is for clients.
The visual depiction provides an overview, while the textual SRS provides the formal, detailed  specification.
There is no difference; they are interchangeable.

explanation: The lecture states, 'Now so far what we have discussed is just a visual depiction but that is not  a specification as such for the requirements. Now we need to have a textual description as I mentioned  before so textual description follows its own format.'

questionText: In the note-taking application example, 'Search in Notebook' is a top-level  functional requirement. Which of these is a sub-function under it?
explanation: The lecture shows a hierarchy for 'Search in Notebook' under which there are '2 sub functions  search by text, search by date.'

questionText: What is the primary characteristic of the 'black box' concept in FRS?

options.text: The internal workings and algorithms are fully exposed.
Only the input and output are known, not the internal implementation.
It refers to a physical device with no visible components.
It means the function is not yet designed.

explanation: The lecture defines it: 'The function in itself appears to be a black box with only an input and  output specified rather than how the function should be implemented?'

questionText: Why is it important to follow consistent naming conventions throughout the  functional requirement specification?

options.text: To ensure clarity and ease of understanding across the lifecycle.
It is not important, any naming is fine.

explanation: The lecture advises, 'However anyone should be followed consistently throughout the life  cycle.' This implies consistency aids clarity and understanding.

questionText: The lecture suggests that functional requirements 'need not be created based on  end user studies'. What does this imply about their origin?

options.text: They can originate from other sources like domain knowledge and client discussions.
They are always derived from non-functional requirements.
They are only relevant for non-interactive systems.

explanation: The lecture states, 'functional requirements need not be created based on end user studies.  Some domain knowledge plus some discussion with the clients may be good starting point to create the  functional requirements.'

questionText: What is the final stage of the software development lifecycle discussed in the  lecture?
explanation: The lecture lists the stages and concludes: 'So once this study stage is complete and we are  assumed of the usability as well as executability of the system we go for deployment and maintenance that  is our last stage.'

questionText: What is the primary concern when developing interactive software, as  highlighted early in the lecture?
explanation: The lecture states, 'Now interactive software again just to recollect refers to a class of software  that are supposed to be used by layman users who are not experts in the technology. For them we need to  take into account various things most importantly user feedbacks at different stages of development.'

questionText: What is the primary outcome of the requirement gathering, analysis, and  specification stage of the interactive system development life cycle?
explanation: The lecture states, "We mentioned that at the end of these activities what we get is a  document which is called software requirement specification or SRS. Now SRS is the outcome of the stage  of requirement gathering, analysis and specification this document is passed on to the next phase to the  next stage of the life cycle the design stage."

questionText: Which of the following information is NOT explicitly mentioned as an ideal  component of an SRS document's cover page in the lecture?
explanation: The lecture lists: "So, in the cover page then what we should keep first this title software  requirement specification doc for student activity monitor and alert generator which is the name of the  system. Then version number then date on which the version on which this version is created. Then the  people who have created it prepared by so and so place where it is created and finally if there is some  mentor." Detailed functional requirements are part of the main body, not the cover page.
