questionText: What section is recommended for better organization and lists the document's  content in sections and subsections?
explanation: The lecture states, "Then comes; the content section so here for better organization ideally  you should include one content table of contents. Which; will list out the content of the document in the  form of sections, and sub sections as you can see here in this document there are several sections."

questionText: According to the lecture, what is the purpose of including a revision history in  an SRS document?

options.text: To provide a brief history of document versions for record keeping

explanation: The lecture explains, "Next ideally you should include in your SRS some revision history. As I  mentioned the document may have gone through several iterations before it is finalized so each, iteration  is a version. So how many versions have been created a brief history can be given... So ideally in a SRS  document you should list this revision history for record keeping."

questionText: What is one of the primary purposes of the SRS document, as stated in the  lecture, regarding its interaction with customers?

options.text: To serve as a user manual
To be proposed to a customer for their approval

explanation: The lecture states, "This document is primarily intended for intended to be proposed to a  customer for their approval and as a reference for developing the first version of the system for the  development team."

questionText: In the "Document Conventions" section, what information is typically provided  for each term or notation used?
explanation: The lecture describes, "So it is a table having 2 columns one is the term or the notation used  another one is the definition of that particular term."

questionText: What kind of information is expected to be explained in the "Project Scope"  subsection of an SRS document?

options.text: The need and objective for the project in brief

explanation: The lecture states, "Then in the third subsection of the introduction section the project scope  is reported. Ideally you should do that also so it says that this software is meant to be deployed in an IT  enabled large classroom environment... so in under the project scope subsection you explain the need and  objective for this project in brief."

questionText: The "Student Activity Monitor and Alert Generator" system is described as a  "top-up" on an already existing system. What does this imply about its product  perspective?

options.text: It is a completely new system replacing all existing functionalities.
It assumes certain functionalities are already handled by an existing system and adds new  features.
It is a standalone system with no dependencies.
It is a prototype that will be discarded after initial testing.

questionText: What specific sensors are mentioned in the lecture as being leveraged by the  "Student Activity Monitor and Alert Generator" system to determine student  attention?
explanation: The lecture states, "Then comes, the product leverages the sensors such as gyroscope  proximity sensor, accelerometer in the devices used by the students which determine factors such as  orientation, distance from user shaking frequency which enable the system to determine the attention of  students and alert the instructor accordingly."

questionText: For the "Student Activity Monitor and Alert Generator" system, how many user  classes were identified?
explanation: The lecture states, "For this system there are 2 user classes identified instructor and student."

questionText: What is the described operating environment for the "Student Activity Monitor  and Alert Generator" system?
explanation: The lecture states, "The environment is an IT enabled large classroom where both the above  user classes carry their devices."

questionText: What specific constraint was explicitly mentioned regarding the "Student  Activity Monitor and Alert Generator" system's design and implementation?

options.text: The system must be compatible with all operating systems.
The system is forbidden to use the camera for measuring attention.

explanation: The lecture states, "The next subsection is design and implementation constraints if there are  any constraints that are likely to be faced by the teams for the above purpose of implementing the app we  are forbidden to use the camera for measuring the attention."

questionText: Which of the following is an assumption made about the "Student Activity  Monitor and Alert Generator" product, as per the lecture?

options.text: It will always be used on mobile phones with basic configurations.
It will always be used on mobile phones that have enough performance (efficient  performance-wise).
It requires no existing system for slide display.
It can function without any sensors.

questionText: Which type of interface requirement specifies that the UI should be organized  and work-oriented rather than having fancy style and animation?
explanation: The lecture states, "The UI should be more focused on being organized and work oriented  rather than having fancy style and animation the interface should have rigorous error management."

questionText: What is a key hardware interfacing requirement for student mobile devices in  the "Student Activity Monitor and Alert Generator" system?

options.text: They must have a built-in printer.
They should have all necessary sensors like gyroscope, accelerometer, and proximity sensor  with enough specification.
They must have a physical keyboard.
They should only run on a specific brand of device.

explanation: The lecture states, "The student’s mobile devices should have all the necessary sensors like the  gyroscope, accelerometer, and proximity sensor with enough specification to handle the task at hand."

questionText: Regarding software interfaces, what does the lecture mention about the data  collected by student devices?

options.text: It must be stored locally on the student device indefinitely.
It has to be transported to the instructor's device.
It is directly uploaded to a cloud server without passing through the instructor's device.
It is only used for internal device diagnostics.

questionText: What is mentioned about encryption concerns for the "Student Activity Monitor  and Alert Generator" system's communication interface?

options.text: Encryption is a top priority due to global exposure.
Encryption concerns are not humongous because the application is exposed to a limited  environment.
All data must be encrypted with military-grade algorithms.
Encryption is handled by the operating system automatically.

questionText: Which of the following components are considered MANDATORY for a  functional requirement specification, according to the lecture?
explanation: The lecture states, "So rational description these are optional but ID name, input and output  are mandatory."

questionText: What common mistake in specifying functional requirements' input and output  is highlighted in the lecture?
explanation: The lecture repeatedly points out, "So this type of action words is to be avoided in specifying  output as well as input." and "Action words make those look like processes rather than inputs and outputs  so that to be strictly avoided."

questionText: What is the first top-level function listed for the instructor user class in the  example SRS?
explanation: The lecture states, "So let us start with the first user class that is the instructors for an  instructor what are the functions that are to be supported by the system. So first function is start class  session it should be supported by the device by the system."

questionText: In the functional requirement hierarchy for the instructor, the function "Real  time individual student attention statistics" is a sub-function of which higher-level  function?
explanation: The lecture describes the hierarchy: "Now under this top level function we have second level  1.1 establish connection for instructor... The next function which is under this second level function  established connection is real time individual student attention statistics. So by the numbering we can  understand where in hierarchy it stands so it is ID is FR INS 1.1.1". This means it's under 1.1.

questionText: Which of the following is explicitly mentioned as a type of non-functional  requirement in the lecture?
explanation: The lecture states, "A separate and dedicated section is there on non-functional requirements  such as performance requirements, security requirements, software quality attributes and so on."

questionText: What is a specific performance requirement mentioned for the "Student  Activity Monitor and Alert Generator" system regarding real-time statistics?

options.text: The program must update statistics once a day.
The program must update the real-time statistics at a fast enough pace.
The program should only handle 10 students at a time.
The program must store all historical data indefinitely.

questionText: Why are encryption concerns for the "Student Activity Monitor and Alert  Generator" system considered "not humongous"?

options.text: Because the data is not sensitive.
Because the environment is local or limited to the classroom.
Because the system uses a proprietary encryption method.
Because students are not allowed to access the internet.

explanation: The lecture states, "Since the environment is local or limited to the classroom no security  precaution or encryption of data is necessary because it is to be executed over a small area network."

questionText: What is a software quality attribute mentioned in the lecture for the SRS  example?

options.text: The system should be visually appealing.
The code should be modular and well written.
The system must be compatible with all legacy hardware.
The system should have a low memory footprint.

questionText: When specifying the output of a functional requirement, such as "related course  page is opened," what advice does the lecturer give?

options.text: Always include the action word "is opened" for clarity.
Simply state "related course page" and avoid action words.
Provide a detailed process description of how it opens.
Omit the output entirely if it's obvious.

explanation: The lecture explicitly states, "Now one thing you should note here is although it is mentioned  related course page is opened this part of the statement is not required because it is talking about some  process rather than an output. So when you are specifying some output you should not mention about the  process that this is open this is closed. Instead you should simply say what is opened here related course  page that is good enough whether it is opened or not open that need not be mentioned. So this type of  action words is to be avoided in specifying output as well as input."

questionText: Which two components of a functional requirement are described as optional  but beneficial to include?

questionText: Which of the following is NOT a subsection listed under the "Overall  Description" section in the example SRS?

questionText: After the SRS document is finalized, to which stage of the life cycle is it passed  on?

questionText: The lecture mentions that usability requirements are a type of:

questionText: What is the first top-level function listed for the student user class in the  example SRS?

questionText: What is the name of the system for which the example SRS document is created?

questionText: The lecture mentions that the instructor can view student attention data in two  ways. What are they?

To allow the instructor to take attendance.

questionText: In the document conventions, what does "DESC" refer to?

questionText: A performance requirement states that the program must be able to handle the  information of the entire class. What specific number of students is mentioned as an  example for a full attendance?
explanation: The lecture states, "The program must be able to handle the information of the entire class a  full attendance almost 90 students and also individually without any glitch."

questionText: The lecture identifies "exits the current course page and closes all impending  connections" as a "bad way of writing" for an output specification. What is the core  issue with this phrasing?

options.text: It uses too many technical terms.
It includes action words that describe a process.

explanation: The lecture states, "Now here lots of action words are used exits closes so this type of output is  to be avoided. So it has to be refreshed avoiding the action word so this is a bad way of writing so in this  document I will show you the good things as well as the bad things."

questionText: What advice is given regarding the sections and subsections discussed in the  example SRS document?

options.text: All sections and subsections must be present in every SRS document.
Only functional requirements are mandatory, others are optional.
You have to choose depending on your application area what sections and subsections to  keep.
The structure is fixed and cannot be altered.

explanation: The lecture states, "one thing you should keep in mind is whatever sections and subsections  are discussed in this example document need not be present in every document. So you have to take a call  on which interfacing requirements you want to highlight and which are not very relevant." (This applies  generally to sections/subsections).

questionText: What is considered the "most important component" of any SRS document?
explanation: The lecture states, "Most important component is of course the functional requirements;  which lists out the functions that are to be there or to be supported by the product to achieve the  objectives."

questionText: The lecture mentions that some usability requirements can be converted into  what type of requirements?
explanation: The lecture states, "Also keep in mind that some of the usability requirements can be actually  represented as functional requirements which we shall see through examples in later part of the course."

questionText: What is the rationale provided for the "Establish Connection for Instructor"  function?

options.text: To allow the instructor to share files.
Without connection between devices, information cannot be communicated.

explanation: The lecture states, "DESC description says establish connection with the students present  currently in the class and rational is without connection between the devices information cannot be  communicated so we need this function."

questionText: Besides attention determination and alert generation, what other functionality  is expected from the system for the instructor?

options.text: Allowing the instructor to see a summary of data collected during lecture.

explanation: The lecture states, "The application should also allow the instructor to see the summary of the  data collected during lecture which shall be helpful during feedback sessions and grading."

questionText: In the document conventions, what does "DEP" refer to?
explanation: The lecture states, "Rat convention refers to rational the short from of DEP dep refers to  dependency."

questionText: What is a performance requirement related to error messages when a  connection is lost?

options.text: Time to give the error message on losing a particular connection should be minimal.
Error messages should be logged only.
Error messages should be sent to the system administrator.

explanation: The lecture states, "Time to give the error message on losing a particular connection should  be minimal so it should be fast response."

questionText: The lecture discusses a potential issue if cameras were used for attention  monitoring. What was this issue?

options.text: Cameras would consume too much battery.
Students might exploit sensors to portray themselves as paying attention even when they  are not.
Cameras would violate student privacy laws.
Cameras would not work in low light conditions.

explanation: The lecture states, "The students might exploit the sensors used to portray themselves as  paying attention even when they are not. So what it tells is that? The attention can be monitored by the  teacher by simply utilizing the smartphone cameras present in each student’s device however that is  forbidden. That is not to be used because the students can manipulate the camera feed and create a feed  which look like they are paying attention whereas in reality they are not."

questionText: What was the main objective of this lecture regarding SRS documents?

options.text: To discuss a full SRS document, its creation, components, and appearance.
To compare different software development methodologies.

explanation: The lecture states, "But in this lecture what we are going to discuss is a full SRS document how  it is created what are the components present in it how it looks. And so on because so far we have  discussed the concepts related to SRS document in a piecemeal manner. Let us now try to put them  together and see the whole document for better understanding of the documentation process."

questionText: What is the primary concern in interactive systems, as described in the lecture?

options.text: Ease of use for laymen persons

explanation: In interactive systems, the primary concern is to make it 'easy to use' for laymen persons,  which is formally referred to as usability.

questionText: The formal notion of 'easy to use' is referred to as what in the context of Human- Computer Interfaces?
explanation: The lecture states that 'easy to use' has a more formal notion which is called usability, a more  standardized way of saying the same thing.

questionText: Which of the following is NOT one of the initial stages in the software development  life cycle for interactive systems discussed in the lecture?
explanation: The initial stages mentioned are requirement gathering, analysis and specification, design,  prototyping, and early evaluation. Deployment and maintenance comes after usability issues are resolved.

questionText: The cycle consisting of design, prototyping, and early evaluation is generally  called what?
explanation: The lecture explicitly states that the cycle of design, prototyping, and early evaluation is  generally called the 'design prototype evaluate cycle'.

questionText: In the context of interactive systems, 'design' refers to which two distinct things?

options.text: Interface and interaction, and the actual system

explanation: The lecture clarifies that design refers to both the design of the interface and interaction  (user's view) and the design of the actual system (developer's view).

questionText: Which type of design, according to the lecture, typically requires prototyping and  evaluation?
explanation: The lecture states, 'system design may not require prototyping but interface design requires  prototype and evaluation'.

questionText: What is the limitation of code testing in the interactive software development  lifecycle?

options.text: It only checks for security vulnerabilities.
It only tells about execution efficiency, not usability.
It is too costly and time-consuming.

explanation: The lecture explains that code testing will only tell about the execution efficiency of the  system, not its usability.

questionText: What is an 'empirical test' also known as, in the context of usability?
explanation: To know the usability, another type of test called empirical test is carried out, also known as  empirical study or empirical research.

questionText: Why should frequent revisions based on empirical studies be avoided if possible?

options.text: They introduce too many new bugs.
They are not effective in improving usability.
Usability study is a costly affair and leads to cost and time overrun.
They delay the deployment stage unnecessarily.

explanation: The lecture notes that 'usability study or empirical study is a costly affair. So if we need to  frequently revise our design and go for empirical study then it will lead to cost and time over run.'

questionText: What are the two types of requirements referred to in the lecture?
explanation: The lecture states, 'Here by requirements what we are referring to are 2 types of  requirements one is usability requirements other one is functional requirement'.

questionText: What is the example system used for the case study on usability requirement  gathering?
explanation: The example system discussed is 'a calendar app which we have mentioned in the earlier  lectures'.

questionText: Who is the primary user group for the calendar app in the case study?
explanation: The objective is to build a calendar app 'primarily meant to be used by students with the  objective of helping them in their various academic activities'.

questionText: Usability requirements are categorized as what type of requirements?
explanation: The lecture states, 'usability requirement is one sort of non-functional requirement along  with many other non-functional requirements'.

questionText: Which method was discussed in detail for gathering requirements in an earlier  lecture and is assumed for the calendar app case study?
explanation: The lecture mentions, 'One of those which we have discussed in details in earlier lecture is  contextual inquiry. So for our example system let us assume that we are going to perform a contextual  inquiry'.

questionText: What is the primary objective of contextual inquiry?

options.text: To conduct structured interviews with users.
To observe users in their work setting or context of use.
To analyze system logs for user behavior.
To gather quantitative data through questionnaires.

explanation: Contextual inquiry is an 'observation based primary objective is to observe the users in their  work setting or context of use'.

questionText: How many stages are involved in carrying out contextual inquiry, as described?
explanation: The lecture states, 'Now there are 5 stages to carry out the observations'.

questionText: Which stage of contextual inquiry involves communicating with potential users  to explain the purpose and gain their willingness to be observed?
explanation: In the 'initiate' stage, 'we start the process in the form of communicating with the potential  users for their time and to explain to them the purpose so that they are less anxious and willing to let us  observe their behavior'.

questionText: In which stage of contextual inquiry are observations actually recorded?
explanation: The 'execution stage or execute stage here we actually observe and record our observations'.

questionText: What is the difference between active and passive observation modes in  contextual inquiry?

options.text: Active mode uses video, passive mode uses audio.
Active mode involves user interaction, passive mode does not.
Active mode has the observer physically present, passive mode records observations for later  viewing.
Active mode is for functional testing, passive mode is for usability testing.

explanation: In active mode, 'the observer is physically present in the work setting and observes'. In  passive mode, 'the observer is not present somehow the observations are recorded and the recordings are  viewed later'.

questionText: What happens in the 'Close' stage of contextual inquiry?

options.text: Thank you notes are sent to participants and incentives are given.

explanation: In the 'close' stage, 'some thank you notes are sent to the participants so that they are formally  notified about the closure of the process as well as they are given some incentives'.

questionText: Which method is used to analyze data collected during contextual inquiry, as  discussed in the lecture?
explanation: The lecture states, 'one method we have learnt in some details that is the affinity diagram  method'.

questionText: How many steps are involved in the Affinity Diagram Method?
explanation: The Affinity Diagram Method 'involves 5 steps'.

questionText: What does 'Generate Idea' mean in the Affinity Diagram Method?

options.text: Brainstorming new features for the app.
Converting observations into short descriptions or notes.
Creating a list of potential users.

explanation: 'Generate idea' means 'after observations whatever you observe from there take note or  generate ideas' and 'converting observations to such short descriptions is what is being referred to as  generate ideas'.

questionText: What is the purpose of 'Display ideas' in the Affinity Diagram Method?

options.text: To make ideas easy to visualize, e.g., on sticky notes on a wall.
To store ideas in a database.

explanation: 'Putting up those ideas in some form so that they are easy to visualize is what is being  referred to as display those ideas so here to display we probably can use one wall on which we can paste  those sticky notes.'

questionText: What is the third stage of the Affinity Diagram Method?
explanation: The third stage is 'brainstorming stage where the ideas which are displayed needed to be  sorted into groups'.

questionText: When performing contextual inquiry for the calendar app, what specific  condition was emphasized regarding the observation of calendar usage?

options.text: Users were observed using calendars for personal and academic activities.
Users were observed using calendars only for academic activities.
Users were observed using only mobile calendars.
Users were observed using calendars in a lab setting.

explanation: The lecture states, 'we have observed them using these calendars only for academic activities  not for any other activities because we are interested only for such work settings'.

questionText: Why is replicating the work setting important in contextual inquiry?

options.text: To reduce the cost of the study.
To ensure the data collected is relevant for the intended system's use.
To make the observation process faster.

explanation: The lecture emphasizes, 'So replicating work setting is very important in contextual inquiry  method' because if data is collected for another scenario, 'that data may not be relevant for the particular  work setting that you wish to have while the system is used'.

questionText: Which of the following was a hypothetical observation made about calendar  usage by all users?

options.text: All users used calendars to check meeting dates.
All users used calendars to set reminders.
All users used mobile apps for scheduling.
All users used calendars to check upcoming deadlines.

explanation: One observation noted was 'the calendar is used by all the users to set reminders'.

questionText: According to the hypothetical observations, what percentage of users used  mobile calendar apps to check day and date and set reminders for assignment  submission?
explanation: The observation states, '3 out of 5 users used mobile calendar app to check day and date and  set reminder for assignment submission'.

questionText: What was observed about all users regarding lecture schedules?

options.text: All users used calendars to check lecture schedule on a particular day.
All users preferred paper-based calendars for lecture schedules.
All users used mobile apps for lecture schedules.

explanation: A hypothetical observation was 'all users use the calendars in whatever form either paper- based desktop or mobile to check lecture schedule on a particular day'.

questionText: When grouping the hypothetical observations for the calendar app, which two  observations were initially grouped under 'Reminder Setting'?

options.text: Checking deadlines and checking meeting dates.
Setting reminders by all users and setting reminders via mobile apps by majority.
Checking lecture schedules and checking meeting schedules.
Checking timetables and checking meeting dates.

explanation: The lecture shows 'all users used calendars to set reminders' and '3 out of 5 users used mobile  apps to set reminders' were grouped together under 'reminder setting'.

questionText: What is a key consideration when interpreting observations made during  contextual inquiry?

options.text: Observations are only valid for the specific work setting in which they were made.
Observations are always generalizable to all contexts.
Observations are primarily for functional requirements.

explanation: The lecture warns, 'whatever observations we made are not universal truths... The  observations are for all types of calendars used in the study if any calendar type is left out then these  observations do not apply to them... we should only claim the validity of the observations with respect to  the specific work setting.'

questionText: What is the final stage of the Affinity Diagram Method?
explanation: The last stage in the affinity diagram method is 'we need to display the final diagram affinity  diagram'.

questionText: Why is precise grouping important in the Affinity Diagram Method?

options.text: It makes the diagram visually appealing.
It ensures that all observations are included.
The more precise the groups are, the easier it is to find an apt header.
It reduces the number of steps in the process.

explanation: The lecture states, 'Now the more precise the groups are the easier it is to find out a header. So  accordingly our grouping activity needs to be very carefully thought out'.

questionText: The lecture mentions that there is no unique way of grouping observations. What  does this imply for the design process?

options.text: Designers should always stick to the first grouping they create.
Designers should keep an open mind and explore alternative grouping schemes.
Grouping should be avoided if possible.

explanation: The lecture advises, 'we should keep always in mind that there is no unique way of grouping.  So whatever grouping scheme we think of there can always be alternative schemes. So we should always  keep our thinking open'.

questionText: What is the purpose of the 'Reflect' stage in Contextual Inquiry?

options.text: To analyze the collected data and obtain results.
To communicate with users about the study's findings.

explanation: The 'Reflect' stage is where 'whatever data we have collected during observations are  analyzed and results obtained'.

questionText: What is the main difference between interactive systems and other software  systems?

options.text: Interactive systems are distinct due to their primary concern for usability and user interaction.
Interactive systems do not require coding.
Interactive systems are only for entertainment purposes.

explanation: The lecture states, 'human computer interfaces or the interactive systems are distinct from  other software systems. In interactive systems primary concern is to make it quote unquote easy to use to  laymen persons.'

questionText: What is the first step in the Affinity Diagram Method?
explanation: The first step of the Affinity Diagram Method is 'Generate Idea'.

questionText: What is the primary goal of designing and implementing Human-Computer  Interfaces?
explanation: The objective in the design and implementation of human computer interfaces is to design  and usable system.

questionText: What does the 'Plan' stage of contextual inquiry involve?

options.text: Planning what to do in the process, preferably in a script.
Sending thank you notes to participants.

explanation: The 'Plan' stage involves planning 'what we are going to do in the process preferably in the  form of a script'.

questionText: Which of the following is NOT a type of calendar observed in the hypothetical  contextual inquiry for the calendar app?
explanation: The lecture mentions observing students using 'paper based calendars as one mode of  calendar then desktop based calendar and also mobile calendars'. Smartwatch calendars are not  mentioned.

questionText: What was a common observation regarding checking deadlines among the users  in the case study?

options.text: Only 1 out of 5 users checked deadlines.
4 out of 5 users used the calendar to check upcoming deadlines.
No users checked deadlines using calendars.
All users preferred manual methods for deadlines.

explanation: One observation was '4 out of 5 users used the calendar to check upcoming deadlines'.

questionText: What was the alternative grouping scheme proposed for the five 'scheduling'  observations?
explanation: The lecture discusses an alternative way of breaking the five observational notes into 'Overall  scheduling' and 'Day wise scheduling'.

questionText: What is the main benefit of the alternative grouping scheme (Overall scheduling  and Day-wise scheduling) over a single 'Work Scheduling' group?

options.text: It provides better cohesion among the notes and more precise headers.
It is easier to draw the final diagram.

explanation: The lecture states, 'Obviously the latter grouping is better because here we can get a better  cohesion among the notes. Whereas in the previous case, when we club together all the 5 observations the  heading does not reflect everything that these observations contain.'

questionText: What is the purpose of creating 'group headers' in the Affinity Diagram Method?

options.text: To assign unique IDs to each group.
To convey the broad message or concept within a group of observations.
To list all individual observations in a group.
To indicate the number of observations in each group.

explanation: The stage is 'assigning some headers which convey the broad message in a group of  observations'.

questionText: What is the next step after creating an affinity diagram, as mentioned at the end  of the lecture?

options.text: Learning what to do with the output and how to specify requirements.

explanation: The lecture concludes by stating, 'Next is what to do with the grouping so that we will cover in  the next lecture... And how to specify the requirements, so that they can be converted easily to  implementable ideas'.

questionText: What is the role of interviews in contextual inquiry?

options.text: They are the primary data collection method.
They are used to clarify certain behavioral aspects observed during observations.
They are conducted only at the 'Close' stage.
They are a substitute for observations.

explanation: To aid the observations, 'the observer may occasionally take recourse to interviews to get  clarifications on certain behavioral aspects of the user system interaction in the work context'.

questionText: What is the main purpose of the calendar app for students?

options.text: To help them in their various academic activities.

explanation: The app is 'primarily meant to be used by students with the objective of helping them in their  various academic activities'.

questionText: Which stage of the software development life cycle for interactive systems comes  immediately after 'coding and implementation'?
explanation: After 'implementing the design in the coding and implementation stage', 'Then the code is  tested for bugs so code testing is another major stage'.

questionText: What is the significance of user input in the design of usable systems?

options.text: It is optional and can be ignored.
It is crucial and requires additional activities to systematically represent the design process.
It only applies to functional requirements.
It is only considered during the deployment phase.

explanation: Usable system design 'requires us to take users into account while designing the system due to  the necessity of taking user input into account lots of additional activities we have to do'.

questionText: Which stage of the interactive software development life cycle is the current  lecture focusing on?
explanation: The lecture explicitly states, 'So among these stages we are currently covering the  requirement, gathering, analysis and specification stage.'

questionText: What is the primary method discussed for gathering usability requirements?
explanation: The lecture states, 'To gather those usability requirements what we did we have gone through  one particular method called contextual inquiry method.'

questionText: Functional requirements are typically derived from which sources?

options.text: Client interactions and prior designer experience

explanation: Functional requirements 'typically comes through interaction with clients as well as through  prior experience of the designer.'

questionText: What is the defined user group for the calendar application case study?
explanation: The application 'is primarily meant to be developed for students who are expected to use it  for academic purpose. So our user group is fixed students more specifically college going students or  students enrolled for higher studies.'

questionText: What does the term 'event' encompass in the context of the calendar app's  academic activities?
explanation: The lecture clarifies, 'I am going to use the term event to actually indicate a host of things  including lectures exams meetings talks. So everything will be termed as event without any further  disambiguation.'

questionText: What is the 'black box assumption' in the context of functional requirements?

options.text: Functions are hidden from the user
Functions are specified in detail, including implementation
Functions process input to generate output without focusing on internal design
Functions are only for aesthetic purposes

explanation: The lecture states, 'we will assume that the functions are black boxes whatever input is given  somehow it is processed and generates the desired output. So we will assume that that output is generated  the function is designed in such a way rather than focusing on how to design the function so that the  output is generated from the input.'

questionText: What are the two main ideas emphasized for managing functional descriptions?

options.text: User interface design and interaction design

explanation: The slides and transcript mention 'Abstraction - identify black box functions to be supported  by the system (with clearly defined input and output)' and 'Decomposition & hierarchy - to better manage  the functional description'.

questionText: What is the purpose of decomposition and hierarchy when defining functions?

options.text: To hide functions from the user
To make things easier to understand and implement
To reduce the number of functions

explanation: The lecture states, 'hierarchy actually makes things easier to understand and implement in  subsequent stages. So decomposition of a function into sub functions and creating a hierarchy is very much  desirable.'

questionText: Which of the following is NOT a requirement for the 'Display Calendar' top-level  function (R1)?
explanation: The 'Display Calendar' function includes viewing months, days, and event listings, and  jumping to specific dates. Synchronizing with email is a separate top-level function (R4).

questionText: For the 'Display Calendar' (R1) function, if the input is a 'month', what is the  expected output?

options.text: List of events for that day

explanation: The SRS for R1 states: 'If the input is month then the output then the output will be days of the  month.'

questionText: What is the input for the 'Display Month' (R1.1) sub-function?
explanation: The SRS for R1.1 states: 'In this case the input is year, the output is months of the year.'

questionText: What is the output for the 'Display Days with Events' (R1.2) sub-function?

options.text: Days of the month, along with day-wise event lists

explanation: The SRS for R1.2 states: 'input is month and output is days of the month along with day wise  event lists if there are any such events.'

questionText: The 'Specific Date View' (R1.3) sub-function takes 'Date' as input. What is its  output?
explanation: The SRS for R1.3 states: 'Input is date, output is events.'

questionText: Which of the following is a sub-function under 'Set Reminders' (R2)?
explanation: The hierarchy for 'Set Reminders' includes 'Create reminders, then edit reminders and then  delete reminders.'

questionText: What is the input for the 'Create Reminder' (R2.1) sub-function?
explanation: The SRS for R2.1 states: 'input which is date event name and time together constitute the  input.'

questionText: The 'Edit Reminder' (R2.2) sub-function allows the user to modify what aspects of  a reminder?

options.text: Such as time or event name

explanation: The description for R2.2 states: 'In this function the user can modify specific reminders such  as time or event name for specific dates.'

questionText: What is the output of the 'Delete Reminder' (R2.3) sub-function?
explanation: The SRS for R2.3 states: 'output is date without the specific reminder.'

questionText: What are the two sub-functions identified for the 'Set Background' (R3) top-level  function?
explanation: The hierarchy for 'Set Background' includes 'set theme and reset theme'.

questionText: What is the input for the 'Set Theme' (R3.1) sub-function?
explanation: The SRS for R3.1 states: 'input is theme image output is app background with choose an  image.'

questionText: The 'Synchronize' (R4) top-level function aims to reflect what kind of events on  the calendar?

options.text: Only events created within the app
Extrinsic events/meetings created with the email account
Only reminders set by the user

explanation: The description for R4 states: 'So that any extrinsic event meeting created with the email  account is also reflected on the calendar with date and time.'

questionText: What are the two sub-functions under the 'Synchronize' (R4) top-level function?
explanation: The hierarchy for 'Synchronize' includes 'attach account and remove account'.

questionText: What is the output of the 'Attach Account' (R4.1) sub-function?
explanation: The SRS for R4.1 states: 'output is the synchronized reminders.'

questionText: What is the output of the 'Remove Account' (R4.2) sub-function?
explanation: The SRS for R4.2 states: 'output is unsynchronized reminder list.'

questionText: In requirement specification, why is it important not to bother about  implementation details like exact input/output format?

options.text: Because it makes the SRS too long
Because those details are decided by the client
To keep the specification abstract and flexible for later design choices
Because it is not relevant to the system's functionality

explanation: The lecture emphasizes, 'in requirement specification we do not bother about implementation  details such as in which format to specify and how to process the information? ... Rather we will keep it as  abstract and flexible as possible so that later on designer can make a choice depending on availability of  platforms, resources, manpower and other things.'

questionText: What is the primary focus when identifying functions for the SRS?

options.text: The exact input and output format

explanation: The lecture states, 'So essentially our focus is what we need rather than how to achieve the  requirement how to do it?'

questionText: Which of the following is considered a non-functional requirement from a system  developer's perspective?
explanation: The lecture states, 'usability requirements are nonfunctional requirements from the point of  view of a system developer.'

questionText: What is the purpose of the 'description' component in an SRS function  specification?

options.text: To clarify the purpose of the function

explanation: The lecture mentions, 'There can be a description also but as I said earlier this can be optional  but ideally it should be there to clarify the purpose of the functions.'

questionText: The interactive software development life cycle stages are performed in a  particular sequence and sometimes form a loop. Which stages form a loop?
explanation: The lecture states, 'third is basically a set of sub stages performed in a loop manner. So the  sub stages are design sub stage, prototyping sub stage, and quick evaluation of prototyping that is another  sub stage. So together they form a cycle which we are calling the design prototype evaluates cycle.'

questionText: What is the primary goal of empirical user testing or usability testing?

options.text: To test the code for bugs
To ensure the system meets functional requirements
To get to know the usability of the end product

explanation: The lecture states, 'Another testing stage follows which is empirical user testing or usability  testing through this testing we get to know usability of the end product.'

questionText: When distinguishing between clients and end-users, what characteristic is  attributed to end-users?

options.text: They are layman users who need not have any technical expertise
They are responsible for system maintenance

explanation: The lecture states, 'End users are layman users who need not have any technical expertise but  they just want to use the system for achieving certain goals.'

questionText: What is the main difference between usability requirements and functional  requirements?

options.text: Usability requirements are for clients, functional for end-users.
Usability requirements are non-functional, functional requirements define system actions.
Usability requirements are gathered through interviews, functional through contextual  inquiry.
Usability requirements are about 'how to do it', functional about 'what we need'.

explanation: The lecture states, 'usability requirements are nonfunctional requirements from the point of  view of a system developer' and functional requirements 'get to specify those requirements in the form of  functions with clearly defined input, output and some optional description of the functions.'

questionText: The SRS document for the calendar app will primarily specify which type of  requirements discussed in this lecture?

options.text: Both functional and usability requirements equally

explanation: The lecture explicitly states, 'this entire thing will constitute the SRS for the calendar app  which will specify the functional requirements for the SRS to re-emphasize the point. So these are only  considering the functional requirements.'

questionText: What is the work context specified for the calendar app for students?
explanation: The lecture states, 'And the work context is also fixed that is academic environments which  include classrooms which includes PR discussion groups and so on.'

questionText: When specifying functions, the lecture advises against thinking of complex  functions. What is the recommended approach instead?

options.text: Combine all functions into one large function
Divide functions into sub-functions and create a hierarchy
Focus only on the top-level functions
Delegate function definition to the coding stage

explanation: The lecture advises, 'we should not think of complex functions instead we try to divide  functions into sub functions up to the level wherever we feel it necessary. And we should strive to create a  hierarchy of such functions and sub functions.'

questionText: What is one additional functionality mentioned for the calendar app, besides  displaying dates and setting reminders?
explanation: The lecture mentions, 'Synchronization with email may be one such functionality'.

questionText: What is the purpose of the 'label' (e.g., R1, R1.1) used in the SRS notation for  functions?

options.text: To represent the level of the hierarchy

explanation: The lecture states, 'note that name is having a label this label is representing the level of the  hierarchy.'

questionText: The 'Display Calendar' function (R1) takes 'Year/Month/Date' as input. What is its  general output?

options.text: Corresponding months, days, or lists of events for a day
A list of all academic events

explanation: The SRS for R1 states: 'Input: Year/Month/Date Output: Months/Days/Event Lists'.

questionText: What is the input for the 'Display Days with Events' (R1.2) sub-function?
explanation: The SRS for R1.2 states: 'input is month and output is days of the month along with day wise  event lists.'

questionText: The 'Set Reminders' (R2) top-level function has an input of 'Date and event details  with time'. What is its output?

options.text: Reminder for the event at the specified time on the specific date

explanation: The SRS for R2 states: 'Output: Reminder for the event at the specified time on the specific  date.'

questionText: What is the description for the 'Create Reminder' (R2.1) sub-function?

options.text: User can associate a specific date and time with a specific academic event.

explanation: The SRS for R2.1 states: 'Description is in this function the user can associate a specific date  and time with a specific academic event.'

questionText: What is the input for the 'Edit Reminder' (R2.2) sub-function?
explanation: The SRS for R2.2 states: 'In this we have input as date and reminder.'

questionText: The 'Set Background' (R3) top-level function takes 'Images' as input. What is its  output?
explanation: The SRS for R3 states: 'Input: Images Output: App background with chosen image.'

questionText: What is the description for the 'Set Theme' (R3.1) sub-function?

options.text: User can choose app background color.

explanation: The SRS for R3.1 states: 'Description: In this function, the user can set app background.'

questionText: What is the input for the 'Synchronize' (R4) top-level function?

options.text: Details of account to synchronize with

explanation: Refer to Week 3 lecture materials.

questionText: What is the description for the 'Attach Account' (R4.1) sub-function?

questionText: What is the input for the 'Remove Account' (R4.2) sub-function?

options.text: Details of account(s) to be removed or un-synchronized

questionText: The lecture emphasizes that in requirement specification, we do not bother about  which of the following?

options.text: The input and output of functions

explanation: The lecture states, 'neither we are interested in finding out the algorithm for this function to  implement nor, we are interested in specifying the exact input and output format.'

questionText: What is the final stage of the interactive software development life cycle  mentioned in the lecture?
explanation: The lecture lists the stages, concluding with 'deployment and maintenance.'

questionText: If problems are found during usability testing, what might occasionally happen?

options.text: It may lead to returning back to the design prototype evaluation cycle

explanation: The lecture states, 'And occasionally it may lead to returning back to this cycle design  prototype evaluation cycle if we find some problems in the usability testing phase.'

questionText: What is the primary distinction made between 'clients' and 'end-users' in the  context of requirement gathering?

options.text: Clients pay for the system, end-users do not.
Clients provide technical specifications, end-users provide aesthetic preferences.
Clients provide requirements for the system, end-users provide requirements for usability.
Clients are internal stakeholders, end-users are external.

explanation: The lecture states, 'along with requirements provided by the clients we also need to know the  requirements of the actual end users... First of all to gather requirements from end users which is likely to  lead to usable systems these requirements we are referring to as usability requirements.'

questionText: How many stages are there in the interactive system development life cycle  (ISDLC) as described in the lecture?
explanation: The lecture states, 'So all together we have 9 stages that make this interactive system  development life cycle.'

questionText: Which stages of the interactive system development life cycle (ISDLC) are  explicitly mentioned as forming a cycle in the lecture?
explanation: The lecture states, 'For example in the design prototype and evaluation stages create a cycle  as shown here in this block.'

questionText: The term 'design' in the context of interactive system development refers to  which two types?

options.text: Design of the system and design of the database
Design of the interface/interaction and design of the system
Design of the user experience and design of the architecture
Design of the software and design of the hardware

explanation: The lecture clarifies, 'when we are talking of the term design. We are actually referring to 2  types of designs one is the design of the interface and interaction that is from the user’s point of view.  Another one is the design of the system which is from the systems point of view.'

questionText: Usability requirements are generally categorized as what type of requirements?
explanation: The lecture explicitly states, 'note here that usability requirement comes under the non- functional requirement.' and 'usability requirements are generally called non-functional requirements.'

questionText: What is identified as the key requirement from the point of view of an  interactive system?
explanation: The lecture states, 'what we have learned is that the key requirement from the point of view  of an interactive system is the usability of the system'.

questionText: For which aspect of design is the usability requirement primarily applicable?
explanation: The lecture mentions, 'usability requirement is applicable for interface and interaction  design. It is not necessarily a requirement for system design'.

questionText: What is the primary method discussed in the lecture for identifying usability  requirements for the calendar application case study?
explanation: The lecture states, 'we have seen how to find out through contextual inquiry usability  requirements for the calendar application.'

questionText: How many stages comprise the process of Contextual Inquiry (CI) as described  in the lecture?
explanation: The lecture states, 'it is a process that comprises 5 stages'.

questionText: What is the first stage of the Contextual Inquiry process?
explanation: The lecture lists the stages: 'it starts with a planning stage where we plan for the overall  inquiry process.'

questionText: What is the primary activity during the 'Execute' stage of Contextual Inquiry?

options.text: Observing users in their natural work setting

explanation: The lecture states, 'In the third stage now we go for actual data collection which means we  observe the users and take note of their behavior, while they perform their tasks in the work setting. If you  may recollect contextual inquiry is primarily an observation of user behavior in a work setting in their  natural work setting.'

questionText: How can observation in Contextual Inquiry occasionally be augmented for  clarification?
explanation: The lecture mentions, 'And occasionally this observation can be augmented with semi- structured interviews for clarification on certain observations.'

questionText: Which specific method for analyzing observed data from Contextual Inquiry is  discussed in the lecture?
explanation: The lecture states, 'we specifically learned about one particular method namely the affinity  diagram method.'

questionText: How many steps are involved in the Affinity Diagram method?
explanation: The lecture states, 'Now in the affinity diagram method again there are 5 stages and through  those stages, we can analyze the data.So what are those 5 steps or stages'.

questionText: What is the first step in the Affinity Diagram method?
explanation: The lecture lists the steps: 'first is generate idea from observation'.

questionText: For whom is the calendar application in the case study primarily meant?
explanation: The lecture states, 'Now the application is meant for students, primarily students enrolled in  colleges and universities for higher studies'.

questionText: What is the specified user context for the calendar application in the case  study?
explanation: The lecture states, 'and the application is meant to help them in their academic activities.'

questionText: In the hypothetical Contextual Inquiry for the calendar app, what types of  calendars were assumed to be used by students?
explanation: The lecture mentions, 'we assumed that the students used a paper-based calendar, a  computer-based calendar. Here by the term computer. So, in the desktops Computers are referred to as  calendars that are available on mobile phones'.

questionText: What was the group heading for the first group of observations in the affinity  diagram for the calendar app case study?
explanation: The lecture states, 'we put them together in a group with a group heading reminder setting.'

questionText: The second group of observations in the affinity diagram, which included  checking upcoming deadlines and meeting dates, was given what group heading?
explanation: The lecture states, 'we put them together under a group with a group heading overall  scheduling.'

questionText: For the third group of observations (checking timetable, lecture schedules,  meeting schedules), what was identified as the common link?
explanation: The lecture states, 'in all the cases as you can see a particular day is a common link so  accordingly, we group them together these 3 observations and provided a group heading for day-wise  scheduling.'

questionText: What are the two main ways to make use of the output from the Contextual  Inquiry process, as described in the lecture?

options.text: Creating user manuals and training materials
Generating marketing strategies and business plans
Coming up with design guidelines or creating functional requirements
Performing competitive analysis and market research

explanation: The lecture states, 'We can actually make use of these observations or rather we can actually  make use of this output of the process in either of the 2 ways. One is either we can come up with a set of  design guidelines or recommendations or principles... The other way of using the output is to create  functional requirements.'

questionText: Based on the 'Overall Scheduling' observations, one design guideline suggested  is that the app should support viewing of upcoming deadlines for assignment  submission for which periods?

options.text: The current day and also for next 7 days

explanation: The lecture provides an example guideline: 'the app resultant app should support viewing of  upcoming deadlines for assignment submission for the current day and also for next 7 days'.

questionText: From the 'Overall Scheduling' observations, another design guideline suggested  is that the app should support viewing of scheduled meetings for which specific  period?
explanation: The lecture provides an example guideline: 'the app should support viewing of scheduled  meetings for the current date.'

questionText: Based on the 'Day-wise Scheduling' observations, a guideline (Guideline 3)  suggests that the final product should support viewing of what on any given day?
explanation: The lecture states, 'One guideline which we can call guideline 3 can be the final product that  should support viewing of the timetable on any given day.'

questionText: Another guideline (Guideline 4) derived from 'Day-wise Scheduling'  observations suggests the calendar app should support viewing of what on any given  day?
explanation: The lecture states, 'That is the calendar app or the product should support viewing of lecture  schedules on any given day.'

questionText: Framing guidelines from Contextual Inquiry output is expected to lead to what  for the final product?
explanation: The lecture states, 'And that in turn is likely to lead to more efficiency effectiveness and  satisfaction of the end product as per the standard definition of usability.'

questionText: Before adding new functions based on the affinity diagram, what were the four  top-level functional requirements identified for the calendar app?

options.text: Display Calendar, Set Reminder, Set Background, Synchronize
Create Event, Delete Event, Edit Event, Share Event
User Login, User Profile, Notifications, Search
View Day, View Week, View Month, View Year

explanation: The lecture states, 'So there were 4 top-level functions display calendar, set a reminder, set  background, and synchronize.'

questionText: Based on the affinity diagram, what new top-level functional requirement was  added to the calendar app's hierarchy?
explanation: The lecture states, 'So based on the observations we can add a top-level function view'.

questionText: What label was assigned to the new top-level functional requirement 'View' in  the hierarchy?
explanation: The lecture states, 'so we are giving it a label R5.'

questionText: What is the specified input for the new top-level functional requirement 'View'  (R5)?
explanation: The lecture states, 'Now its input is any date'.

questionText: What is the specified output for the new top-level functional requirement 'View'  (R5)?
explanation: The lecture states, 'and output is a specific view for that particular date. Now the view map,  the view may be related to the timetable view submission deadlines view, or meeting list view.'

questionText: What is the label for the sub-function under 'View' that allows users to check  day-wise timetables of lectures?
explanation: The lecture states, 'So one sub-function can be timetable viewed accordingly we have given it  a level R5.1.'

questionText: What is the input for the 'Timetable view' (R5.1) sub-function?
explanation: The lecture states, 'Now its input is the date'.

questionText: What is the output for the 'Timetable view' (R5.1) sub-function?
explanation: The lecture states, 'and the output is the timetable for the day'.

questionText: What is the label for the sub-function under 'View' that allows users to check  day-wise assignment submission deadlines?
explanation: The lecture states, 'Similarly, we can have another sub-function deadline view the name is  deadline view label is 5.2'.

questionText: What is the input for the 'Deadline view' (R5.2) sub-function?
explanation: The lecture states, 'Now again its input is date'.

questionText: What is the output for the 'Deadline view' (R5.2) sub-function?
explanation: The lecture states, 'and output is submission deadlines'.

questionText: What is the label for the sub-function under 'View' that allows users to check  day-wise meeting schedules?
explanation: The lecture states, 'There can be a third sub-function as well under the function view which is  meeting schedule. Accordingly, the level is 5.3'.

questionText: What is the input for the 'Meeting schedule' (R5.3) sub-function?
explanation: The lecture states, 'input is debt' (interpreted as 'date' based on context).

questionText: What is the output for the 'Meeting schedule' (R5.3) sub-function?

options.text: List of meetings scheduled on that day

explanation: The lecture states, 'output is list of meetings scheduled on that day'.

questionText: What is the primary purpose of adding new functional requirements based on  observations from contextual inquiry?

options.text: To increase the complexity of the system
To indicate to the design team features beneficial to end-users and improve usability
To reduce the overall development timeline

explanation: The lecture states, 'Now through these requirements, we are indicating to the design team  that these are to be provided as functions of the final product or as features of the final product which will  be very much beneficial to the end users and will lead to improved usability of the product.'

questionText: Is it mandatory to convert usability requirements into functional requirements?

options.text: Only if the client requests it

explanation: The lecture explicitly states, 'it is not mandatory to be able to convert such requirements into  functional requirements' and 'it is not mandatory to be able to convert those requirements into functional  requirements.'

questionText: If usability requirements cannot be converted into functional requirements,  how should they be handled in the Software Requirement Specification (SRS)  document?

options.text: They should be kept as non-functional requirements
They should be moved to the design document
They should be implemented as optional features

explanation: The lecture states, 'So if you are unable to convert usability requirements into functional  requirements then you can keep that requirement as non-functional requirement in the SRS document'.

questionText: What is the most important outcome for the Software Requirement  Specification (SRS) document?

options.text: To be as short as possible
To include both non-functional and functional requirements
To be written only by developers

explanation: The lecture states, 'So what matters most is? At the end you get a software requirement  specification document which includes both non-functional requirement as well as functional  requirements.'

questionText: In the 'Initiate' stage of Contextual Inquiry, what is the primary action?

options.text: Communicating with potential users and authorities

explanation: The lecture states, 'then initiate stage where we start the process by communicating with the  potential users from whom we will collect data as well as their higher authorities in the work setting if any  such authorities exist.'

questionText: What is a key activity during the 'Close' stage of Contextual Inquiry?

options.text: Sending thank you notes to participants

explanation: The lecture states, 'In the fourth stage, we close the observation process by sending preferably  thank you notes to the participants and creating a rapport'.

questionText: After generating ideas from observation in the Affinity Diagram method, what is  the next step?

options.text: Display the ideas on some place

explanation: The lecture lists the steps: 'first is generate idea from observation then display the ideas on  some place'.

questionText: What activity is performed in a team to sort ideas into groups of similar ideas  during the Affinity Diagram method?
explanation: The lecture states, 'then we need to perform brainstorming in a team to sort those ideas into  groups of similar ideas.'

questionText: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle is performed iteratively until what is  achieved?

options.text: A design that no longer has many issues is arrived at

explanation: The lecture states, 'this process goes on iteratively Till we arrive at a design that no longer has  many issues.'

questionText: While usability is a key requirement for interface and interaction design, is it  necessarily a requirement for system design?
explanation: The lecture states, 'usability requirement is applicable for interface and interaction design. It  is not necessarily a requirement for system design'.

questionText: What is the primary concern during the interface design phase of an interactive  system?
explanation: The lecture states, "In interface design primary concern was usability and the design  guidelines were again based on users behavioral characteristics and they were primarily meant to help us  design usable products."

questionText: Which of the following is NOT considered a stage in the interactive system  development life cycle mentioned in the lecture?
explanation: The lecture lists feasibility study, requirement gathering, design, prototyping, early  evaluation, coding and implementation, code testing, empirical study, and deployment and maintenance as  stages. Marketing and sales is not mentioned.

questionText: The "design-prototype-evaluate" cycle primarily refers to the design of which  aspect of an interactive system?
explanation: The lecture explicitly states, "Now this design prototype evaluate cycle primarily refers to the  design of user interfaces."

questionText: According to the lecture, what are the two major issues that designers should be  aware of and address in their design activities?

options.text: Where to start and how to represent

explanation: The lecture identifies "Where to start the process?" and "How to specify it how to represent  it?" as the two major issues.

questionText: What is the primary purpose of the "empirical study" stage in the interactive  system development life cycle?

options.text: To test the code for proper execution
To gather initial requirements from stakeholders
To test the usability of the end product by involving end users
To refine the design based on technical specifications

explanation: The lecture states, "Whereas in empirical study we test usability of the end product by  involving end users in the evaluation of the whole product or software."

questionText: Which method is mentioned for gathering usability requirements?
explanation: The lecture states, "we have learned one particular method that is contextual inquiry."

questionText: What is the role of an "Affinity Diagram" in the requirement gathering and  analysis stage?

options.text: To specify software requirements in a formal document
To collect raw data from users
To analyze data collected through contextual inquiry
To design the user interface layout

explanation: The lecture explains, "Then we have learned the affinity diagram method which works on the  data collected through contextual inquiry to analyze the results of the gathering exercise."

questionText: In User-Centered Design (UCD), design encompasses two distinct concepts. What  are they?
explanation: The lecture states, "when we talk of UCD or user center design now here the design is not a  single idea here design actually encompasses 2 distinct concepts. One is interface design... and second is the  design of the system or code design."

questionText: When does the "design-prototype-evaluate" cycle stop?

options.text: When the coding and implementation stage begins
When the design stabilizes, meaning no further problems are found after evaluation
After a fixed number of iterations, regardless of issues
When the project budget is exhausted

explanation: The lecture states, "The cycle stops when the design stabilizes that means no further problems  are found in the design after the evaluation of the prototypes."

questionText: What is the primary focus in "code design" as opposed to "interface design"?

options.text: Efficiency of implementation and code manageability

explanation: The lecture contrasts them: "In interface design primary concern was usability... But those are  not useful in code design where our primary focus is efficiency of the implementation. Along with that our  primary focus is to make the code manageable."

questionText: Which document serves as the end product of the requirement gathering,  analysis, and specification stage and is used as a basis for code design?
explanation: The lecture mentions, "earlier in the requirement stage we saw that we need to create an SRS  or software requirement specification document as the end product of the stage. Code design actually is  based on the SRS that we create."

questionText: What are the two distinct phases involved in code design?
explanation: The lecture states, "when we talk of code design there are 2 distinct phases are involved the  first one is the preliminary phase or high level design phase. And there is another one that is the detailed  design phase also called module specification document."

questionText: What is identified during the "high-level design" phase of code design?

options.text: Specific data structures and algorithms for modules
User interface elements and their placement
Modules, their control relationships, and interfaces between them
Detailed test cases for code validation

explanation: The lecture states, "in the high level design what we need to do we need to identify the  modules? That means, the units which together constitute the overall system. Then define relationships  between the modules control relationships between the modules how the modules are linked to each other.  And also we need to define interfaces between modules."

questionText: What is the primary focus during the "detailed design" phase of code design?

options.text: Data structures and algorithms for individual modules

explanation: The lecture states, "in the detailed design phase. We turn our attention to the design of  individual modules particularly the data structures and algorithms to be used to implement individual  modules."

questionText: How is interface design typically represented or specified, according to the  lecture?
explanation: The lecture states, "In case of interface design the representation is done with prototypes. So  prototypes effectively give us a language to express the design."

questionText: Why are natural languages generally not suitable for expressing design  specifications?

options.text: They are too formal and rigid.
They lack the necessary vocabulary for technical details.
They are inherently ambiguous and can lead to confusion.
They are difficult for non-technical team members to understand.

explanation: The lecture explains, "natural languages are inherently ambiguous. So natural languages  although can be technically used but are not suitable or preferable to express design languages."

questionText: Which two semi-formal graphical languages are mentioned for specifying  system (code) design?
explanation: The lecture states, "So we learn 2 such languages one is DFD or data flow diagram... Second  one is also a partly graphical language... this is called UML or unified modeling language."

questionText: What is the main characteristic of "generic" design guidelines like  Shneiderman's 8 golden rules or Norman's 7 principles?

options.text: They are very specific to particular products or platforms.
They cover broad aspects of interactive systems at a high level and are small in size.
They are primarily used for code design, not interface design.

explanation: The lecture describes generic guidelines as "very generic in nature that means they patent to  very broad aspects of a design of a usable design and because they are very generic. So they are usually  small in size."

questionText: The 8 golden rules by Ben Shneiderman and 7 principles by Donald Norman  originated during the proliferation of what type of interfaces?
explanation: The lecture states, "Now both these sets actually originated during the proliferation of  graphical user interfaces."

questionText: What does the acronym "WIMP" stand for in the context of graphical user  interfaces?
explanation: The lecture defines WIMP as "Windows, icons, menus and pointers or what we generally call  wimp interfaces."

questionText: How were design guidelines like Shneiderman's 8 golden rules developed?

options.text: Based on empirical data collected over time and behavioral analysis of human users
By adapting existing software engineering principles

explanation: The lecture states, "they were framed based on empirical data collected over a long period of  time and after analysis of that data some behavioral models were formed and out of those models these  guidelines emerged. So they were rooted in behavioral analysis of human users."

questionText: What is an example of a "detailed and specific" set of design guidelines  mentioned in the lecture?

options.text: Human Interface Guidelines for Apple systems

explanation: The lecture mentions, "One example can be the human interface guidelines that was  developed for the apple systems this set of guidelines contained hundreds of individual guidelines which  are primarily meant to build products on apple platforms on apple OS."

questionText: What is the primary characteristic of "prototypes" when used as a language for  interface design?

options.text: They are formal languages with strict syntax.
They are scaled models of the designs.

explanation: The lecture states, "Prototypes are scaled models of the designs when we create prototype we  essentially express the design."

questionText: Which of the following is NOT a way to express code design, according to the  lecture?
explanation: Prototypes are used for interface design, not code design. The lecture lists natural, semi- formal, and formal languages for code design.

questionText: What is the advantage of using semi-formal languages for code design  specification?

options.text: They are as rigorous as formal languages.
They are completely free of ambiguity.
They are partly graphical, easier to understand, and reduce ambiguity compared to natural  languages.
They require no prior knowledge or training.

explanation: The lecture describes semi-formal languages as "Partly graphical language and rather  informal way of expressing things and easier to understand but at the same time it reduces ambiguity."

questionText: The interactive system development life cycle aims to build a system that is  both:
explanation: The lecture states, "through these stages we try to build one interactive system that is  executable as well as usable."

questionText: Usability requirements are categorized as what type of requirements?
explanation: The lecture states, "So the usability requirements are non-functional requirements."

questionText: What is the purpose of the "code testing" stage in the interactive system  development life cycle?

options.text: To evaluate the user interface with end-users.
To ensure the code executes properly along expected lines.
To deploy the system to production.

explanation: The lecture states, "in code testing we test the code for its ability to execute properly along  expected lines."

questionText: When considering "where to start" for interface design, what can aid creative  thinking?

options.text: Strict adherence to formal mathematical models.

explanation: The lecture states, "Implicitly we may be relying on our intuition or our past experience both  may be aiding in our thinking process." and "this creativity can be added by experience... The creative  thinking can also be aided by our intuition."

questionText: What is the primary reason for the continuous revision and updating of design  guidelines, checklists, and heuristics?

options.text: To make them more complex and detailed.
To ensure they remain relevant to new technologies.
To incorporate knowledge gained from their application on building usable products.
To reduce the number of guidelines for simplicity.

explanation: The lecture states, "Based on the knowledge gain these sets were continuously revised  updated so that at the end whatever they contain is proven to be useful for building usable systems."

questionText: Which of the following is a characteristic of "formal languages" for code design  specification?

options.text: They are very rigorous and require mathematical background.
They are easy to understand for all team members without training.

explanation: The lecture states, "Formal languages are the best way to express any design however  because it is a very rigorous expression it requires mathematical background."

questionText: The lecture uses a case study of what type of application to explain the  requirement gathering, analysis, and specification stage?
explanation: The lecture states, "we try to explain that in terms of one case study of an application namely  a calendar application. Primarily to be used by the student community."

questionText: What is the significance of clear and precise communication of ideas from one  stage to another in the software development life cycle?

options.text: It allows new team members to start working without requiring constant consultation.
It reduces the overall project timeline by skipping documentation.
It ensures that only highly experienced team members are involved.
It eliminates the need for any design specifications.

explanation: The lecture emphasizes, "this input that the team gets which is the output of some previous  stage should be clearly understandable. So that the new member can start working on the idea without any  problem without requiring to, consult the member of the team which executed the previous stage that is  very important."
