questionText: Which section of the design document typically contains definitions of specific  terms used throughout the document?
explanation: The glossary of terms section is where specific terms used in the document are defined.

questionText: According to the lecture, what is the ideal way to record the creation date on a  software design document's cover page?

options.text: A single date of final creation
Only the date of the first draft
A history of fast creation, revision, refinement, and final document creation dates
The date of the last review

questionText: In object-oriented design, which of the following are mentioned as the three  major views for representing a design?

options.text: Data View, Process View, Deployment View
Use Case View, Behavioral View, Structural View
Logical View, Physical View, Component View
Static View, Dynamic View, Functional View

The system prompts the player to input their name and age

questionText: What do behavioral diagrams, such as sequence diagrams, primarily illustrate?

How objects behave and interact during runtime

questionText: In a sequence diagram, what does the length of the bar representing an object  indicate?

questionText: The lecture mentions two acceptable sequences for creating design views in a  document. Which of the following represents the sequence *not* followed in this  specific design document, but is considered a 'right way to do'?

To avoid creating a very complex diagram

questionText: Which stage of the software development life cycle for interactive systems is the  current lecture focusing on?

Empirical study, and deployment and maintenance

questionText: What is the primary concern when designing the interface of an interactive  system?

questionText: What is the main difference between testing of the interface (prototyping) and  testing of the code?

options.text: Interface testing is done by developers, code testing by users.
Interface testing involves domain expert users, code testing focuses on bugs after  implementation.
Interface testing is for functionality, code testing is for aesthetics.
Interface testing is a one-time activity, code testing is continuous.

questionText: According to the lecture, what is a common mistake in naming a function like 'f'  for adding two numbers?

options.text: It does not convey any meaning.

explanation: The lecture states, 'One problem is with the name of the function. So, here we have given it a  name f. Now f does not convey any meaning. So, ideally the name of the function should convey some  meaning'.

questionText: What is the recommended practice for naming variables like 'a', 'b', and 's' in the  example code?

options.text: Use single arbitrary characters for brevity.
Name them in a way that conveys their purpose.
Keep them consistent with function names.

explanation: The lecture advises, 'ideally we should name our variables in a way such that they convey the  purpose of those variables'.

questionText: Why is proper indentation important in code?

options.text: It reduces the file size of the code.
It makes the code compile faster.
It is a requirement for all programming languages.

explanation: The lecture states, 'if we follow this type of indentation... that improves readability if  everything is written along the same vertical line then readability is affected.'

questionText: What value do meaningful function names, meaningful variable names, proper  indentation, and documentation add to a program?

options.text: They make the code run faster.
They reduce the need for testing.
They help to understand and maintain a program.

explanation: The lecture explains, 'These things like meaningful function names meaningful variable  names proper indentation and additionally some documentation or comments conveying the purpose of  the statements or the overall function adds lots of values to any program that you are writing. In fact that  helps us to understand and maintain a program in a much better way'.

questionText: What is a key benefit of following standard coding guidelines or practices,  especially in large projects?

options.text: It ensures all code is written by a single developer.
It eliminates the need for code reviews.
It improves readability, understandability, and helps in teamwork.

explanation: The lecture states, 'So, they help in improving readability and understandability most  importantly that helps in teamwork.' It also mentions, 'if a standard is followed if some guidelines are  followed then it is easier to understand and integrate those different pieces of code at the end and test  those. So, it helps in implementing good teamwork.'

questionText: Which naming convention is suggested for global variables?
explanation: The lecture suggests, 'For example global variables may always start with uppercase letters'.

questionText: Where should global variables ideally be kept to make them easy to find?

options.text: In a single or limited number of definition files.
Only within functions where they are used.

explanation: The lecture advises, 'Ideally they should be kept in a single or limited number of definition  files that means they should be kept in one place. So, that it is easier to locate all the global variables used  in your program.'

questionText: What information should typically be included in a module header?

options.text: Only the module's name and creation date.
Module name, creation date, author, modification history, summary, and functions with  parameters.
Only the global variables used in the module.
A list of all external libraries used.

Different functions  supported in the module along with their input output parameters... Global variables if any global  variables are used or modified'.

questionText: What is the recommended naming convention for constants?
explanation: The lecture states, 'constant names may always be in capital letters. So, whenever we are  trying to define some constant we should always use capital letters to name it.'

questionText: When dealing with errors and exceptions, what is crucial for reporting facilities?

options.text: Using different return values for error/success in each function.
Following a consistent standard across all parts of the code.

explanation: The lecture emphasizes, 'we should follow this convention for all functions it should not  happen that. Whatever standard we follow we should follow it  consistently across all the parts of the code.'

questionText: What is a suggested rule of thumb for adding comments to code?

options.text: One comment for every ten source lines.
One comment for every three source lines.
Comments are only necessary for complex algorithms.
No comments are needed if the code is self-explanatory.

explanation: The lecture suggests, 'at least one concise and explanatory comment on average for every  three source lines should be there.'

questionText: What is the purpose of a technical manual accompanying an implementation?

options.text: To provide a high-level overview for users.
To offer a detailed understanding of the code.

questionText: Why should 'cleverly written' or cryptic code be avoided?

options.text: It is less efficient in terms of execution speed.
It is difficult to understand and maintain, affecting teamwork.
It often contains more bugs than straightforward code.
It is not supported by modern compilers.

explanation: The lecture states, 'such quote unquote cleverly written codes are very difficult to understand  and difficult to maintain only the programmer knows what the code does and others if they are asked to  understand it others find it very difficult to understand the code that affects maintainability and eventually  that affects team spirit.'

questionText: What is an example of a 'cleverly written' code style that should be avoided?

options.text: Writing the entire code in one line.
Splitting large functions into smaller ones.

explanation: The lecture gives an example: 'many coders actually take pride in writing very cryptic and  incomprehensible code such as writing the entire code in one line.'

questionText: What are 'obscure side effects' in the context of coding?

options.text: Errors that are easy to detect during compilation.
Changes to parameters, global variables, or I/O operations that are not apparent from reading  the code.
Features that are intentionally hidden from the user.
Code that runs in the background without user interaction.

explanation: The lecture defines them as 'obscure side effects which are not apparent from the reading of  the code.' and mentions they are 'generally associated with the function calls which involves modification  of parameters modification of global variables and input output operations.'

questionText: Why should obscure side effects be avoided?

options.text: They make the code run slower.
They affect understanding of the code because changes are not apparent.

explanation: The lecture states, 'Clearly obscure side effects affect understanding of the code because we  do not know what is going to be changed.'

questionText: Why should the same identifier not be used for multiple purposes?

options.text: It always leads to syntax errors.
It makes understanding the code difficult, even if it improves memory efficiency.
It is a feature of object-oriented programming.
It is only acceptable for temporary loop variables.

explanation: The lecture explains, 'We often use the same identifier to denote several temporary entities...  Now this is often done to take into account memory efficiency issues but then while it may improve  memory efficiency understanding the code becomes difficult.'

questionText: What is a recommended guideline for the length of a function?

options.text: Functions should be as long as necessary to complete a task.
Function length should not be more than 10-15 lines of code.
Functions should always be exactly 50 lines long.
There is no guideline for function length.

explanation: The lecture suggests, 'One guideline you can follow is that function length should not be more  than 10 lines of code. So, under a function ideally you should not use more than 10 lines of codes. If you are  having functions involving more than 10 lines of codes then those are usually difficult to understand and  most likely such functions can be split into multiple functions... any function whose length is more than 10  or maybe more than 15 lines of code probably is a good candidate to be split into multiple functions.'

questionText: What is a consequence of having lengthy functions?

options.text: They lead to a larger number of bugs.
They reduce the overall code size.

explanation: The lecture states, 'Also if you have lengthy functions then there is high likelihood that it will  lead to larger number of bugs that is quite obvious the more lengthier the code is the possibility of having  more bugs increases that is true for functions as well.'

questionText: Why should the indiscriminate use of 'goto' or branching statements be avoided?

options.text: They are outdated and not supported by modern languages.
They make the program unstructured and difficult to understand the logical flow.

explanation: The lecture explains, 'Otherwise it is very difficult to understand the logical flow in the code  because there are too many branching and that eventually makes a program unstructured and difficult to  understand.'

questionText: What is the overall goal of following good coding practices?

options.text: To write code that is only understandable to the original programmer.
To write code that is easier to understand, maintain, and modify.
To maximize the use of complex language features.
To minimize the number of lines of code at all costs.

explanation: The lecture concludes, 'So, it is always advisable to follow these things and write a good code  which is easier to understand easier to maintain and easier to modify.'

questionText: Which of the following is NOT a stage in the interactive system design life cycle  discussed?
explanation: The lecture lists: 'requirement gathering analysis and specification stage then design  prototyping and evaluation cycle coding and implementation stage code testing stage empirical study stage  and deployment and maintenance stage'. Marketing and sales strategy is not mentioned.

questionText: What is the purpose of prototyping in the design stage of interactive systems?

options.text: To test the usability of the interface.

explanation: The lecture states, 'design of the interface where primary concern is usability and there we  require prototyping and evaluation of prototyping to come up with an interface that is usable.'

questionText: When testing code, what kind of problems are typically identified?
explanation: The lecture mentions, 'testing the code to see whether the code has any problem in terms of  bugs that may be syntactic problems semantic problems. So, in testing we find out these problems'.

questionText: What is a characteristic of good coding practices regarding readability and  maintainability?

options.text: They make the code readable and maintainable.
They are only for experienced programmers.
They are optional for small projects.

explanation: The lecture states, 'it is not necessary that you always follow good coding practice often we  have the tendency to write codes in a very brief manner in a very convoluted manner or avoid certain  things which makes the code readable and maintainable. So, it is always advisable to follow good writing  practices'.

questionText: In the C code example for adding two numbers, what was identified as a problem  with the variable names 'a', 'b', and 's'?

options.text: They did not convey any meaning.
They were not declared as integers.

explanation: The lecture points out, 'name of the variables like a b s again ideally we should name our  variables in a way such that they convey the purpose of those variables in contrast here we have given  some arbitrary name. So, they do not convey any meaning.'

questionText: What is the effect of writing all code along the same vertical line without  indentation?

options.text: It makes the code more compact.

explanation: The lecture states, 'if everything is written along the same vertical line then readability is  affected.'

questionText: What is a suggested way to make global variables distinguishable?

options.text: Keep them in a separate file without any special naming.
Always start them with uppercase letters or use prefixes/suffixes like 'gbl_'.
Use only single-letter names for them.

explanation: The lecture suggests, 'global variables may always start with uppercase letters and we can  also use prefix or suffix to indicate group global variables such as gbl_name or name_gbl.'

questionText: What is a good practice regarding the number of global variables?

options.text: Use them indiscriminately and in large numbers.
Keep the number of global variables limited.

explanation: The lecture advises, 'when we are using global variable we should remember that it is better  to keep the number of global variables limited. So, we should not use them indiscriminately and in large  numbers'.

questionText: What is the purpose of including modification history in a module header?

options.text: To track who accessed the module.
To summarize changes made to the module and the dates they occurred.
To list all functions within the module.
To provide a high-level overview of the module's content.

explanation: The lecture states, 'modification history. So, if you have made any changes in the module. So,  that history that is the dates on which the changes are made and what are the changes those things should  be summarized and kept in the header.'

questionText: What is important to maintain when naming variables, functions, and modules?
explanation: The lecture emphasizes, 'we should follow some convention and maintain consistency in  naming that is very important while giving names to different components of a program.'

questionText: What is a standard error condition reporting facility mentioned for functions?

options.text: Returning a random integer for errors.
Returning 0 for error and 1 otherwise, consistently.
Printing error messages to the console.

explanation: The lecture suggests, 'for example functions may return a 0 for error or 1 otherwise  consistently.'

questionText: What should be done with exceptional situations like 'division by zero' during  execution?

options.text: They should be ignored as they are rare.
They should be identified and taken care of.
They should be reported only to the system administrator.
They indicate a fundamental flaw in the programming language.

explanation: The lecture states, 'Wemust take care of exceptional situations. So, while execution takes place  if there is some exception such as division by zero then that should be taken care of so we have to identify  and take care of exceptions that may happen during execution of any code.'

questionText: What is the primary purpose of documentation in code?

options.text: To increase the file size of the code.
To explain the meaning, purpose, and content of the code.
To make the code more complex.

explanation: The lecture states, 'every portion of the code should have proper documentation to explain  the meaning purpose and content of the code.'

questionText: What is the difference between a user manual and a technical manual?

options.text: User manual is for developers, technical manual is for end-users.
User manual is for high-level view, technical manual is for detailed understanding of the code.
User manual is for installation, technical manual is for troubleshooting.
There is no significant difference; the terms are interchangeable.

explanation: The lecture clarifies, 'User manual is for high level view of the code whereas technical manual  is for detailed understanding of the code.'

questionText: Which of the following is considered a bad coding practice?

options.text: Writing very cryptic and incomprehensible code.

explanation: The lecture advises avoiding 'very cryptic and incomprehensible code' and 'cleverly written  codes' because they are 'very difficult to understand and difficult to maintain'.

questionText: What is the main issue with coding styles that 'obscure meaning and hamper  understanding'?

options.text: They make the code more secure.
They are preferred by experienced programmers.

explanation: The lecture states, 'So, those coding styles can obscure meaning and hamper understanding as  I already said and max maintenance difficult that is pretty obvious from the previous example.'

questionText: What is an example of an obscure side effect related to global variables?

options.text: A global variable being explicitly modified by a function.
A global variable changing its value without being apparent from the code, in a called module.
A global variable being declared as constant.
A global variable being used only for logging purposes.

explanation: The lecture gives an example: 'a global variable may have changed obscurely in a called  module which we are not aware of so, we are probably dealing with a changed value rather than the  original value that. We thought is stored in the global variable.'

questionText: What is the primary reason to avoid using the same identifier for multiple  purposes?

options.text: It makes the code less memory efficient.
It makes understanding the code difficult.
It is a modern programming language restriction.

explanation: The lecture states, 'while it may improve memory efficiency understanding the code becomes  difficult.'

questionText: What is the consequence of using variables that do not have descriptive names  indicating their purpose?

options.text: It makes the code run faster.
It makes the code more compact.
It makes the code harder to understand.
It is a common practice in professional development.

explanation: The lecture states, 'Also we should not use variables that do not have descriptive names  indicating purpose. So, this is already mentioned earlier naming convention should be such that the name  should reflect the purpose.' If names don't reflect purpose, understanding is hindered.

questionText: If a function's length exceeds 10-15 lines of code, what is a recommended action?

options.text: Leave it as is, as length doesn't matter.
Add more comments to explain its complexity.
Rewrite it in a more complex, 'clever' way.

explanation: The lecture suggests, 'most likely such functions can be split into multiple functions you  probably instead of splitting have joined them together and put them under same function. So, any  function whose length is more than 10 or maybe more than 15 lines of code probably is a good candidate to  be split into multiple functions.'

questionText: What is the main problem with too many branching constructs in code?

options.text: They make the code unstructured and difficult to understand the logical flow.
They are only present in older programming languages.
They increase the memory footprint of the program.

explanation: The lecture states, 'Otherwise it is very difficult to understand the logical flow in the code  because there are too many branching and that eventually makes a program unstructured and difficult to  understand.'

questionText: Which of the following is a good coding practice to follow?
explanation: The lecture summarizes, 'That is follow indentation naming conventions, module headers,  handle errors and exceptions and use documentations.'

questionText: What is the primary reason for organizations or companies to have their own  coding guidelines?

options.text: To ensure consistency and quality across projects.
To make code harder for competitors to understand.
To reduce the need for testing.

explanation: The lecture mentions, 'Now organizations or companies may have their own guidelines or  standards that they would like to follow however there can be some generic guidelines that everybody can  follow.' The context of teamwork and maintainability implies consistency and quality.

questionText: What is the first step in the software development life cycle for interactive  systems?
explanation: The lecture lists the stages: 'requirement gathering analysis and specification stage then  design prototyping and evaluation cycle coding and implementation stage code testing stage empirical  study stage and deployment and maintenance stage'.

questionText: What is the purpose of the 'design of the system or code design' stage?

options.text: To create prototypes for usability testing.
To plan the structure and logic of the software.

explanation: The lecture mentions 'The other design is the design of the system or code design we covered  both these concepts in our earlier lectures.' This stage logically precedes writing the actual code.

questionText: What does the lecture suggest about the general guidelines for coding?

options.text: They are not relevant in modern programming.
It is always advisable to be aware of them.
They should be strictly ignored if they conflict with personal style.

explanation: The lecture states, 'however there can be some generic guidelines that everybody can follow.  So, it is always advisable that we are at least aware of those general guidelines.'

questionText: What is one primary reason for performing code testing?

options.text: To ensure the code is aesthetically pleasing.
To check if the code follows proper syntax for compilation.
To determine the execution speed of the code.
To automatically fix all bugs in the code.

explanation: The lecture states that one primary reason for testing is 'to know if the code is written with  proper syntax... So, that we can compile the code and create the executable program.'

questionText: Besides syntactical correctness, what other aspect does code testing aim to verify  regarding the code's behavior?

options.text: Its ability to perform what it is meant to perform, producing expected outcomes.
Its adherence to strict memory usage limits.

explanation: The lecture mentions, 'Secondly we need code testing to know if the code performs what it is  mean to perform. So, it produces the expected outcome after execution that means we need to test whether  the code is logically accurate.'

questionText: Why is it important for code testing to check if the code follows conventions?

options.text: To reduce the overall file size of the code.
To ensure the code is compatible with older software versions.
So that others can understand and maintain the code, facilitating team effort.
To automatically generate documentation for the code.

explanation: The lecture states, 'we need to go for code testing to know if the code follows convention. So,  that others can understand and maintain the code. Now this is very important not only syntactical and  semantical correctness we also need to test code specifically keeping in mind the maintainability of the  code.'

questionText: Which tool is typically used to check for syntactical correctness of code?
explanation: The lecture explains, 'We rely on the compilers which typically comes in built with the  integrated development environments... to check for syntactical correctness of your code.'

questionText: For which types of testing are IDEs or inbuilt compilers generally not helpful?

options.text: Logical correctness and compatibility with conventions.
Memory leak detection and performance profiling.

explanation: The lecture states, 'The other two testing situations namely testing for logical correctness and  testing for compatibility with convention our IDEs or the inbuilt compilers cannot be of any help.'

questionText: What are the two broad categories of code testing methods discussed?

options.text: Review-based code testing and execution-based code testing.

explanation: The lecture clearly states, 'Now there are two broad categories of methods one is review  based code testing other one is execution based code testing.'

questionText: Which characteristic best describes review-based code testing?

options.text: Relatively less rigorous but quick and cost-effective.

explanation: The lecture describes review-based testing as 'relatively less rigorous but they are also quick  methods for testing of your code... offers a cost effective strategy.'

questionText: When is review-based testing typically carried out?

options.text: After a module is successfully compiled and all syntax errors are eliminated.
Only after the entire system is fully integrated.
As the final step before product release.

explanation: The lecture states, 'generally such testing are carried out after a module or an unit is  successfully compiled and all syntax errors are eliminated.'

questionText: Code inspection is described as being somewhat similar to which prototype  evaluation method?
explanation: The lecture mentions, 'code inspection which is somewhat similar to heuristic evaluation that  we have earlier seen during our discussion one valuation of prototypes.'

questionText: What is the primary objective of code inspection?

options.text: To measure the execution time of the code.
To check for violation of coding standards using a checklist.
To automatically refactor the code for better performance.
To simulate user interactions with the software.

explanation: The lecture states, 'team members will check the code for violation of coding standards. So,  we have a checklist of standards to be followed.'

questionText: Code walkthrough is similar to which prototype evaluation method?
explanation: The lecture states, 'The other method is code walkthrough again this is similar to the cognitive  walkthrough method that we have seen or discussed earlier in the context of evaluation of prototypes.'

questionText: In a code walkthrough, what do team members typically do to identify logical  errors?

options.text: They run automated scripts on the code.
They manually execute the code (hand execution) for representative test cases.
They review the code for syntactical errors.
They interview the original programmer about the code's logic.

explanation: The lecture explains, 'each team member will manually execute the code this is often called  hand execution... for some test cases which are to be representative test cases to identify logical errors.'

questionText: How do review-based testing methods like inspection and walkthrough help in  the development process?

options.text: They guarantee a completely bug-free system.
They save development time by quickly identifying many errors.
They eliminate the need for any further formal testing.
They automatically generate all necessary test cases.

explanation: The lecture states, 'So, eventually they help us save development time... idea is that we  identify as many errors as possible with this quick method.'

questionText: What is the core process of formal or rigorous execution-based testing?

options.text: Manually reviewing code for adherence to standards.
Providing a program with test inputs (test cases) and observing its behavior/output.
Discussing code logic with a team without running it.
Using compilers to check for syntax errors.

explanation: The lecture describes formal testing as 'consists of providing the program a set of test inputs  which popularly is known as test cases and then observing the behaviour of the program in other words  the output primarily.'

questionText: According to the lecture, a test case can be considered a triplet (I, S, O). What  does 'S' represent?

options.text: State of the system at the time of providing input data.

explanation: The lecture defines a test case as 'a triplet I, S and O. So, here I stands for the input data S  stands for the state of the system at the time of providing input data and O stands for the expected output.'

questionText: For simplicity in subsequent discussions, the lecture states that a test case will  generally be considered as which doublet?
explanation: The lecture states, 'However for simplicity in subsequent discussion we will consider only the  doublet I and O.'

questionText: What is a 'test suit'?

options.text: A set of all test cases with which a given software is to be tested.
A tool for automating code compilation.

explanation: The lecture defines a test suit as 'a set of all test cases with which a given software is to be  tested.'

questionText: Is it generally possible to guarantee that a software is completely error-free after  testing?

options.text: Yes, with sufficient resources and time.
No, it is practically impossible due to large input data domains.
Only for very small and simple programs.
Yes, if automated testing tools are used exclusively.

explanation: The lecture states, 'In practice it is generally not possible to guarantee that a software is  completely error free after testing... because input data domain... are generally very large in size.'

questionText: Given that exhaustive testing is impractical, what should be the objective of  formal testing?

options.text: To find every single minor bug.
To identify all major problems and increase confidence in the system.
To prove that the software is perfect.
To minimize the number of test cases used.

explanation: The lecture clarifies, 'our objective should be we test to find out major problems... However  our objective should be to identify all major problems... In that way it is more practical to reduce important  defects in a system and that in turn is likely to increase confidence in a developed system.'

questionText: What is the implication of selecting test cases randomly?

options.text: It guarantees a comprehensive test suit.
It ensures all errors will be uncovered efficiently.
They may not necessarily contribute to the significance of a test suit or detect additional  defects.
It always leads to a smaller, more effective test suit.

explanation: The lecture states, 'If we select the test cases randomly then they not necessarily contribute to  the significance of a test suit that means they need not detect additional defects not already detected by  other test cases.'

questionText: What is the key principle for designing an effective test suit?

options.text: It should be as large as possible.
It should be designed randomly to cover all possibilities.
It should be carefully designed using systematic approaches.
It should only include test cases that are easy to implement.

explanation: The lecture emphasizes, 'So, the implication is test suit should be carefully designed it should  not be decided randomly... Now this careful design of test suit requires some systematic approaches.'

questionText: In functional testing, how are test cases designed?

options.text: Using knowledge of the internal structure of the code.
Based on the performance requirements of the system.
Using only the functional specification of the software, without internal knowledge.
By observing user behavior in a live environment.

explanation: The lecture states, 'functional testing here test cases are designed using only functional  specification of the software. That means without any knowledge of the internal structure.'

questionText: Which type of testing treats each function as a 'black box,' considering only the  declaration part and ignoring the internal structure?
explanation: The lecture explains, 'one popular way of going for this type of testing is black box testing. As  the name suggests we treat each function as a black box only the declaration part is considered the internal  or structural part is ignored.'

questionText: How are test cases decided in structural testing?

options.text: Based on the external user interface design.
Based on the knowledge of the internal structure of the code.
Based on the project's budget constraints.
Based on the feedback from marketing teams.

explanation: The lecture states, 'Here we decide the test cases based on the knowledge of the internal  structure of the code.'

questionText: White box testing is an example of which type of systematic testing approach?
explanation: The lecture states, 'one example is white box testing which is a kind of structural testing.'

questionText: Which type of testing is described as more formal and rigorous, aiming to  identify more errors?
explanation: The lecture states, 'The other testing method is the execution based testing which is more  formal and rigorous testing method with the objective of identifying more and more errors.'

questionText: What is the primary difference in objective between code inspection and code  walkthrough?

options.text: Inspection focuses on performance, walkthrough on security.
Inspection checks coding standards, walkthrough identifies logical errors with test cases.
Inspection is automated, walkthrough is manual.
Inspection is for small modules, walkthrough for entire systems.

explanation: The lecture states, 'in case of inspection primary objective is to check if the code follows the  standards. And in case of code walkthrough primary objective is to check if there are any logical errors  with respect to some representative test cases.'

questionText: Which review-based testing method specifically helps to conform to good coding  practices, aiding maintainability and portability?
explanation: The lecture states, 'Code inspection helps to conform to good coding practices which in turn  helps in maintainability and portability of the code.'

questionText: Which review-based testing method allows developers to quickly identify logical  errors, assuming representative test cases are chosen?
explanation: The lecture states, 'Code walkthrough on the other hand allows the developers to quickly  identify logical errors.'

questionText: Review-based testing is described as being good for 'early evaluation.' What does  this early evaluation help to do?

options.text: Clean up the code before more rigorous and formal testing is done.
Determine the market viability of the software.

explanation: The lecture states, 'Such type of testing s are good for early evaluation similar to prototype  evaluation and testing. Now that early evaluation helps us to clean up the code before more rigorous and  formal testing is done.'

questionText: In rigorous program testing, if the program fails to behave as expected, what is  noted for later debugging and correction?

options.text: The total number of lines of code.
The conditions or inputs under which failure occurs.
The estimated time to fix the bug.

explanation: The lecture states, 'If the program or the code fails to behave as expected... the conditions or  the inputs under which failure occurs are noted for letter debugging and correction.'

questionText: Why is exhaustive testing impractical for most real-life software products?

options.text: It is too expensive to hire enough testers.
The possible input data values are likely to be extremely large or infinite.
Compilers cannot handle such large test suites.
Users prefer to find bugs themselves.

explanation: The lecture states, 'Exhaustive testing is impractical because possible input data values are  likely to be extremely large or infinite.'

questionText: What does the lecture imply about the relationship between the total number of  test cases in a suit and its testing effectiveness?

options.text: A larger number of test cases always indicates higher effectiveness.
The total number of test cases does not necessarily indicate testing effectiveness.
Effectiveness is solely determined by the speed of execution.
Only automated test cases contribute to effectiveness.

explanation: The lecture states, 'So, the total number of test cases in a suit not necessarily indicates the  testing effectiveness where effectiveness is defined in terms of identification of major or important defects  in the system.'

questionText: In the example of finding the larger of two integers, a larger test suit with three  test cases failed to detect the error. What was the reason for this failure?

options.text: The test cases were too complex.
The test cases were not carefully chosen to be representative.
The code itself was too simple for the test suit.
The test suit was too small.

explanation: The lecture concludes from the example, 'So, the moral of the story is if you do not choose  your test cases carefully and create your test suit appropriately then no matter whether the test suit is  larger or not you may not be able to identify the error.' The three test cases all tested the x > y condition,  missing the x < y condition where the bug was.

questionText: If you are testing a function add(int a, int b) by only providing various integer  inputs and checking the sum, without looking at how the addition is implemented  internally, what type of testing are you performing?
explanation: The lecture describes functional testing as designing test cases 'using only functional  specification of the software. That means without any knowledge of the internal structure.' This matches  the description.

questionText: In Black Box Testing, which part of a function is primarily considered?
explanation: The lecture states, 'in black box testing... only the declaration part is considered the internal  or structural part is ignored.'

questionText: What is a defining characteristic of White Box Testing?

options.text: It focuses on the user interface.
It is performed without any knowledge of the code's internal structure.
It designs test cases based on the internal structure of the code.
It is always an automated process.

explanation: The lecture states, 'In case of structural testing we design test cases based on the internal  structure of the code an example of functional testing is black box testing. An example of structural testing  is white box testing.'

questionText: In the interactive system development life cycle, which stage immediately  precedes the 'coding and implementation' stage, as discussed in the lecture?

options.text: Design of the system or code design.

explanation: The lecture states, 'Subsequently we covered design of the system or code design. Then we  discussed in the previous lecture the coding and implementation stage.'

questionText: The design, prototype, and evaluation cycle is primarily meant for interface  design, keeping what in focus?
explanation: The lecture states, 'Now this design prototype evaluation cycle is primarily meant for  interface design keeping usability in focus.'

questionText: Checking if code follows conventions is crucial for which aspect of software  development, especially in a team environment?

options.text: Enabling others to understand and maintain the code.

explanation: The lecture states, 'we need to go for code testing to know if the code follows convention. So,  that others can understand and maintain the code... this is required to implement a team effort.'

questionText: What is the role of review-based testing in relation to more rigorous and formal  testing?

options.text: It replaces the need for formal testing entirely.
It serves as a pre-processing step to clean up the code before formal testing.
It is only used for final product validation.
It is a more rigorous method than formal testing.

explanation: The lecture states, 'Now that early evaluation helps us to clean up the code before more  rigorous and formal testing is done. So, eventually we have to go for some somewhat rigorous and formal  testing but before that we can apply the code review methods to kind of preprocess the code and clean up  some important errors.'

questionText: When a program fails during rigorous testing, what is the immediate action taken  regarding the failure?

options.text: The conditions or inputs under which failure occurs are noted for later debugging.
The entire test suit is redesigned.

explanation: The lecture states, 'If the program or the code fails to behave as expected... the conditions or  the inputs under which failure occurs are noted for letter debugging and correction.'

questionText: In the test case triplet (I, S, O), what does 'O' stand for?
explanation: The lecture defines 'O' as 'the expected output.'

questionText: Since exhaustive testing is impractical, what is the goal when designing a test  suit?

options.text: To make it as small as possible.
To make it of reasonable size and uncover as many existing errors as possible.
To ensure it only tests the most common scenarios.
To use only automatically generated test cases.

explanation: The lecture states, 'Then we must design test suit that is of reasonable size and can uncover as  many errors existing in the system as possible that is our goal.'

questionText: How does proper and systematic testing contribute to the confidence in a  developed system?

options.text: It guarantees that no bugs will ever appear in the future.
It ensures the system will never fail in any real-life situation.
It helps identify major problems, allowing rectification and increasing confidence.
It reduces the need for user training.

explanation: The lecture states, 'In that way it is more practical to reduce important defects in a system and  that in turn is likely to increase confidence in a developed system.'

questionText: The lecture compares code inspection to a 'checklist type evaluation.' What is  being checked against this checklist?
explanation: The lecture states, 'code inspection is kind of similar method where we have a set of  predetermined things to check... team members will check the code for violation of coding standards.'

questionText: In code walkthrough, the 'usage scenario' is referred to as what?
explanation: The lecture states, 'So, like cognitive walkthrough there are some usage scenario which we  call test cases.'

questionText: What is a common characteristic of the input data domain for most real-life  software products that makes exhaustive testing difficult?

options.text: It is always fixed and small.
It is generally very large in size.
It is only composed of numerical values.

explanation: The lecture states, 'input data domain that means the set of values that can act as input for  most of the real life software products are generally very large in size.'

questionText: Why is a systematic approach required for designing test suits?

options.text: To ensure the test suit is as large as possible.
To guarantee that all minor bugs are found.
To effectively identify important problems or defects.
To reduce the overall cost of software development to zero.

explanation: The lecture states, 'we have to adopt a very appropriate method which has to be carried out in  a very systematic manner. So, that we are able to identify the important problems or important defects  with the system that is our goal.'

questionText: What does the lecture explicitly state is not a practical way to think of testing?

options.text: Guaranteeing a completely error-free software after testing.
Using systematic approaches for test case design.
Increasing confidence in a developed system.

questionText: What are the two broad groups of approaches for code testing mentioned in the  lecture?

questionText: Which statement accurately describes review-based testing methods compared  to execution-based testing methods?

options.text: Review-based methods are more formal and rigorous.
Execution-based methods are quicker and more cost-effective.
Review-based methods primarily aim to identify major errors quickly.

explanation: The lecture states, 'Now review based testing methods are as we have noted in our earlier  lectures quick cost effective way to test your code. In contrast, execution-based is described as 'more  formal and more rigorous in nature where we mostly focus on analyzing the code internally as well as  externally and accordingly we design test cases and then go for testing'.

questionText: Code walkthrough is conceptually similar to which prototype evaluation  method?

questionText: Code inspection is conceptually similar to which prototype evaluation method?

questionText: What is the primary objective of code walkthrough?

options.text: To check for adherence to coding standards.
To discover algorithmic and logical errors in the code.
To identify common types of errors caused by oversight.
To ensure proper storage allocation and deallocation.

explanation: The lecture states, 'Here the main objective is to discover algorithmic and logical errors in the  code. Remember we mentioned two error types one is logical error other one is violation of conventions or  standards in Code walkthrough our primary objective is to identify logical errors rather than the violation  of Standards.'

questionText: What is the primary objective of code inspection?

options.text: To discover algorithmic and logical errors.
To check for adherence to coding standards and common errors due to oversight.
To simulate execution of the code by hand.

questionText: In code walkthrough, what does 'simulate execution of the code by hand' mean?

Manually tracing the execution of statements and functional execution for given inputs.
Using a specialized hand-held device to run the code.
Having a team member physically act out the code's logic.

questionText: What characteristic is desirable for test cases chosen during a code  walkthrough?

In contrast,  for code inspection, it says, 'this method is more suitable to check for adherence to the coding standards.'  and 'primary objective is not to identify logical errors rather identify common mistakes that happen during  programming as well as adherence to coding standards whether that is being followed or not.'

questionText: Where do companies typically derive the checklist used for code inspection?

questionText: A formal program testing method, such as execution-based testing, typically  involves which of the following?

Providing a set of test inputs and observing program behavior

questionText: What is a common challenge when designing test suits for real-life programs?

options.text: The program's internal structure is always unknown
The input data domain is typically very large or infinite
Test cases are always randomly selected

explanation: The lecture states, 'possible input data to a program in real world real life are generally  extremely large or infinite in size.'

questionText: Why are randomly selected test cases generally not considered effective for  designing a test suit?

options.text: They are too difficult to generate
They do not necessarily detect additional defects not already detected
They always lead to a very large test suit
They are only suitable for white-box testing

explanation: The lecture states, 'Randomly selected test cases are not necessarily good they not necessarily  contribute to significance of test suit that means randomly selected test cases need not detect additional  defects not already detected by other test cases.'

questionText: What does the lecture state about the number of test cases and testing  effectiveness?

options.text: A larger number of test cases always guarantees more errors uncovered
The number of test cases is a direct indication of testing effectiveness
A large number of randomly selected test cases does not guarantee uncovering most errors
Fewer test cases are always better for efficiency

explanation: The lecture states, 'number of test cases is not an indication of testing effectiveness that  means if we go for a large number of test cases which are selected at random does not guarantee that all or  even most of the errors will be uncovered.'

questionText: Given the limitations of random test cases, what is implied about test suit design?

options.text: Test suits should be as large as possible
Test suits should be designed following a systematic approach
Test suits should only use boundary values
Test suits are unnecessary for informal testing

explanation: The lecture concludes, 'our test suit should be carefully designed not decided randomly. So,  we should do something to design the test suit. This in turn implies that test should be designed following a  systematic approach.'

questionText: In functional testing, how are test cases designed?

options.text: Using knowledge of the internal structure of the software
Based on the functional specification of the software without internal knowledge
By randomly selecting inputs from the entire domain
Primarily by observing system state changes

explanation: The lecture states, 'we design test cases using only functional specification of the software that  means without any knowledge of the internal structure of the software.'

questionText: In black-box testing, how is the software visualized?

options.text: As a transparent system with visible internal workings
As a set of functions where each function is treated as a black box
As a single, monolithic block of code
As a series of interconnected modules with known interfaces

explanation: The lecture states, 'we visualize the software as consisting of a set of functions each function  is treated to be a black box we do not know how the function the output or how the function gets its work  done.'

questionText: What is the primary focus of black-box testing?

options.text: The internal algorithms and data structures
The input and output of the function
The system state changes during execution

explanation: The lecture states, 'we are only bothered about the input and output of the function.'

questionText: What distinguishes structural testing from functional testing?

options.text: Structural testing focuses only on input/output
Structural testing uses random test cases
Structural testing involves full awareness of the internal structure of the software
Structural testing is an informal method

explanation: The lecture states, 'in structural testing we are fully aware of the internal structure of the  software that means how the codes get executed and test cases are designed using this knowledge of the  internal structure.'

questionText: Structural testing is also known by what other name?
explanation: The lecture states, 'This approach the structural testing approach is also known as white box  testing approach.'

questionText: When performing black-box testing on a function like `add(int a, int b)`, what  knowledge is assumed?

options.text: The specific arithmetic operations performed inside `add`
That it takes two integers as input and produces an integer output
The exact number of CPU cycles it takes to execute

questionText: What are the two main approaches discussed for designing test cases in black- box testing?

options.text: Equivalence class partitioning and Boundary value analysis

explanation: The lecture states, 'Two main approaches are there. Equivalence class partitioning and  boundary value analysis'.

questionText: What is the fundamental idea behind equivalence class partitioning?

options.text: To randomly select inputs from the entire domain
To divide the input domain into non-overlapping subsets where program behavior is similar
To test only the boundary values of the input
To analyze the internal code structure for test case generation

explanation: The lecture explains, 'we have a domain of input or input domain which is a set and we  divide it into or partition it into subsets each subset is called an equivalence class and generally these  subsets are non overlapping.' And 'the behaviour of the program is similar for every input data belonging  to an equivalence class'.

questionText: What is the purpose of dividing the input domain into equivalence classes?

options.text: To increase the total number of test cases
To ensure every possible input is tested individually
To assume similar program behavior for inputs within a class, allowing fewer test cases

explanation: The lecture states, 'We do that assuming that the behaviour of the program is similar for  every input data belonging to an equivalence class'. This allows selecting one input from each class to  represent the whole class.

questionText: If a program's behavior is similar for all elements in an equivalence class, how  many input values from that class are typically chosen for testing?
explanation: The lecture states, 'if we test our code with any one value of equivalence class of an  equivalence class then that is as good as testing with all input values belonging to that class.'

questionText: What is the ultimate objective of partitioning the input domain into equivalence  classes?

options.text: To make the test suit infinite
To increase the complexity of testing
To keep the size of the test suit finite

explanation: The lecture states, 'in that way we can keep the size of our test suit finite that is the objective  of partitioning input domain into equivalence classes.'

questionText: How is Boundary Value Analysis (BVA) related to Equivalence Class Partitioning  (ECP)?

options.text: BVA is an alternative to ECP
BVA is a completely separate testing method
BVA is closely related to the partitioning approach and complements it
BVA is only used in white-box testing

explanation: The lecture states, 'The other thing that we should consider is boundary value analysis this is  closely related to the partitioning approach.'

questionText: Why is Boundary Value Analysis important in conjunction with Equivalence Class  Partitioning?

options.text: Because program behavior is always consistent at boundaries
Because the behavior may change at the boundaries of equivalence classes
To reduce the total number of test cases
To randomly select more effective test cases

explanation: The lecture states, 'at the boundary of the classes or the corresponding sets the behaviour  may change.'

questionText: When designing test cases using black-box testing, what is the recommended  approach regarding Equivalence Class Partitioning and Boundary Value Analysis?

options.text: Use ECP or BVA, but not both
Use ECP first, then BVA if ECP fails
Approach the problem as both ECP and BVA
Only use BVA for complex systems

explanation: The lecture states, 'in fact they are not either or instead what we do is while designing test  cases we approach the problem as a problem of equivalence class partitioning as well as a problem of  boundary value analysis both are there it is not either or.'

explanation: The lecture states, 'Such testing methods are informal meaning they mostly evaluates code  such methods mostly evaluate code qualitatively.'

options.text: For early evaluation when the code is built
After all other testing methods have failed

explanation: The lecture states, 'Now such methods are typically good for early evaluation when the code is  built but when we want to quickly check whether there are some issues with the code.'

questionText: What is a key difference in how code is handled between review-based and  execution-based testing?

options.text: Review-based uses computers, execution-based uses manual checks
Review-based involves actual execution, execution-based does not
Review-based does not execute code, execution-based requires actual execution

questionText: What is the dual objective for designing a test suit, considering the large input  domain?

options.text: To maximize the size of the test suit and use random inputs
To have a reasonable size and uncover as many errors as possible
To only test successful execution paths

explanation: The lecture states, 'We must design test suit that is of reasonable size and can uncover as  many errors existing in the system as possible.'

The entire test suit is redesigned

questionText: When applying black-box testing, what assumption is made about the software's  internal workings?

options.text: Full knowledge of the internal structure is available
The internal structure is completely irrelevant and ignored
Partial knowledge of the internal structure is used
The internal structure is treated as a 'black box' with unknown workings

explanation: The lecture states, 'we visualize the software as consisting of a set of functions each function  is treated to be a black box we do not know how the function the output or how the function gets its work  done. So, we have no knowledge of the internal structure'.

questionText: Why is it stated that one should not rely *entirely* on review-based code testing?

options.text: Because it is informal and qualitative, not rigorous enough for final validation
Because it cannot detect any errors

explanation: The lecture mentions, 'One issue with the review based code testing is that... Such testing  methods are informal meaning they mostly evaluates code such methods mostly evaluate code  qualitatively.' questionText: When partitioning an input domain into equivalence classes, what is a general  characteristic of these subsets?
explanation: The lecture states, 'this set we can partition into subsets like this generally non overlapping  subsets those subsets are equivalence classes.'

questionText: In the simplified definition of a test case (I, O), which component of the original  triplet (I, S, O) is explicitly *not* considered?
explanation: The lecture states, 'we will assume that test case represents only a doublet I and O and we will  not consider S in our discussion.'

options.text: It guarantees detection of all defects
It ensures the test suit is of reasonable size
It may not detect additional defects not already found
It is the most systematic approach

explanation: The lecture states, 'Randomly selected test cases are not necessarily good they not necessarily  contribute to significance of test suit that means randomly selected test cases need not detect additional  defects not already detected by other test cases.'

questionText: What are the two conflicting conditions that lead to practical issues in test suit  design?

options.text: Large input size vs. uncovering many errors

explanation: The lecture states, 'Now these two conflicting conditions one is large input size another one is  uncovering as many errors as possible leads to some practical issues.'

explanation: The lecture states, 'the outcome of each of these stages is a detailed document.'

options.text: Actual execution with defined inputs and observation of behavior/output

questionText: What is NOT a characteristic of review-based code testing?
explanation: The lecture explicitly states, 'In review based testing we do not really execute the code with a  computer'.

questionText: The primary goal of Equivalence Class Partitioning is to:

options.text: Ensure every single input value is tested
Reduce the number of test cases while maintaining test coverage

explanation: The lecture explains that by assuming similar behavior within a class, one value can  represent the class, thus keeping the test suit finite and manageable, which implies reducing the number of  test cases while still covering different behaviors. 'in that way we can keep the size of our test suit finite  that is the objective of partitioning input domain into equivalence classes.'

questionText: Boundary Value Analysis should be applied because:

options.text: All inputs within an equivalence class behave identically
Program behavior might differ at the edges of equivalence classes
It is a standalone alternative to equivalence class partitioning
It helps in understanding the internal code logic

explanation: The lecture states, 'at the boundary of the classes or the corresponding sets the behaviour  may change. questionText: What does 'black box' imply in testing?

options.text: Its internal structure is fully transparent
Its internal structure is unknown or irrelevant to test case design
It is a system with no inputs

explanation: The lecture states, 'we visualize the software as consisting of a set of functions each function  is treated to be a black box we do not know how the function the output or how the function gets its work  done. So, we have no knowledge of the internal structure'.

questionText: Why is a systematic approach to test suit design emphasized over random  selection?

options.text: Systematic approaches guarantee a smaller test suit
Randomly selected test cases are not effective in uncovering additional defects and a large  number doesn't guarantee coverage
Systematic approaches are only for formal testing

explanation: The lecture explains that random test cases 'need not detect additional defects not already  detected by other test cases' and 'number of test cases is not an indication of testing effectiveness that  means if we go for a large number of test cases which are selected at random does not guarantee that all or  even most of the errors will be uncovered.' This leads to the conclusion that 'our test suit should be  carefully designed not decided randomly. So, we should do something to design the test suit. This in turn  implies that test should be designed following a systematic approach.'

questionText: What stage of the Interactive System Development Life Cycle (ISDLC) is currently  being discussed in the lecture?
explanation: The lecture explicitly states, 'currently we are discussing code testing.'

questionText: What are the two broad categories for designing a code testing process?
explanation: The lecture identifies two broad ways to test code: 'one is review based and the other one is  execution based.'

questionText: Which of the following is a primary characteristic of review-based code testing?

options.text: It always requires execution of the code.
It focuses on quantitative performance metrics.
It identifies qualitative issues like conformance to coding standards.
It is typically performed after formal testing.

explanation: Review-based code testing yields 'qualitative issues that are there in the code which include  conformation with the coding standards conventions and presence of common errors.' It is also noted that  'it is not mandatory to execute the code.'

questionText: What is the main purpose of review-based code testing?

options.text: To identify as many issues as possible before more rigorous testing.
To measure the exact performance of the code.
To generate a final report for stakeholders.

explanation: The lecture states, 'The purpose of review based code testing is to identify as many issues as  possible before we go for more rigorous and formal testing.'

questionText: Execution-based code testing primarily involves:

options.text: Asking evaluators to read through the code.
Using a set of test cases which are input-output pairs.
Analyzing the internal structure of the code without running it.
Focusing on coding standards and conventions.

explanation: In execution-based code testing, 'We generally use a set of test cases which is input output  pair for a given input the output is mentioned and then we execute the code with the input to see whether  the desired output is generated or not.'

questionText: Black-box testing designs test cases based on:

options.text: The internal structure of the code.
The algorithms used in the code.

explanation: The basic idea of black-box testing is to 'design test cases based on only input output values  rather than the design or the internal structure of the code.'

questionText: Black-box testing is also known as:
explanation: The lecture mentions, 'one is black box testing or functional testing other one is white box  testing or structural testing.'

questionText: White-box testing designs test cases with full knowledge of:

options.text: The internal structure of the code.

explanation: White-box testing involves 'design test cases with the full knowledge of how the output is  produced that means we are aware of the internal structure of the code.'

questionText: What are the two primary methods used in black-box testing to design test cases?

options.text: Functional decomposition and Data flow analysis
Equivalence class partitioning and Boundary value analysis

explanation: In black-box testing, 'there are two ways using which we can design the test cases one is the  equivalence class partitioning idea and the other one is boundary value analysis.'

questionText: The core idea behind Equivalence Class Partitioning (ECP) is to:

options.text: Partition the input domain into subsets where the program behaves similarly.
Randomly select a large number of test cases.

explanation: ECP involves partitioning the input domain into 'subsets each subset is called an equivalence  class with the idea that the behaviour of the program for any element of an equivalence class is same.'

questionText: What is the main benefit of using Equivalence Class Partitioning?

options.text: It eliminates the need for any other testing methods.
It reduces the number of test cases to a manageable number.
It provides a detailed analysis of the code's internal logic.

explanation: The lecture explains that ECP helps 'manage the number of inputs to be considered for testing  and we are trying to reduce the number to a manageable number.'

questionText: If equivalence classes are not properly defined, what is the consequence?

options.text: The program will automatically correct itself.
The assumption that testing with one value is enough will not hold.

explanation: The lecture warns, 'If we do not do it properly then definitely this assumption will not hold  and our testing will be flawed.' The assumption is that 'testing code with any one value of an equivalence  class is as good as testing with all input values belonging to that class.'

questionText: A test case, as described in the lecture, should be in what format?

options.text: A description of the expected behavior.

explanation: The lecture states, 'our test cases should be in the form input and output... this is the doublet  of the form input and output.'

questionText: For a program computing the square root of an integer in the range 0 to 5000  (inclusive), what was the most obvious initial equivalence class proposed?

questionText: Why was the initial single equivalence class (0-5000) for the square root program  considered insufficient?

options.text: It required too many test cases.
It did not account for invalid inputs like negative numbers or numbers outside the range.
It only worked for perfect squares.
It was too complex to implement.

explanation: The lecture points out that this initial class failed to test for inputs like '-9' or '5001 onwards',  which are outside the specified valid range.

questionText: For the square root program (0-5000), what were the three improved equivalence  classes suggested?
explanation: The improved solution proposed three classes: 'set of all negative integers,' 'set of all integers  in the range of 0 to 5000 both inclusive,' and 'set of all integers that are larger than 5000.'

questionText: With the three improved equivalence classes for the square root program, how  many test cases would the test suit minimally comprise?
explanation: The lecture states, 'Test suit must include representative input from all equivalence classes  that means in this case there will be three test cases comprising of the test suite one is for the three  equivalence classes.'

questionText: In the improved square root example, if an invalid input like -5 is provided, what  is a more informative output than 'null'?

options.text: The absolute value of the square root.

explanation: The lecture suggests that if output is 'null' for an invalid input like -5, 'we may like to provide  to the user a message mentioning invalid output rather than simply printing null.'

questionText: For the program computing the intersection point of two straight lines (y=mx+c),  what is the input?

options.text: Two integer pairs (m1, c1) and (m2, c2).

explanation: The input for this program is described as 'two integer pairs m1 c1 and m2 c2 each pair  defines a straight line assuming the form y equal to mx + c.'

questionText: Why would a single equivalence class of 'set of all lines' not work for testing the  line intersection program?

questionText: How do Equivalence Class Partitioning (ECP) and Boundary Value Analysis  (BVA) complement each other in black-box testing?
